q: A corrupted Master Boot Record on a legacy BIOS system is rewritten with
explain: /fixmbr writes a fresh MBR; /fixboot writes a new boot sector; both are WinRE staples for legacy boot.

q: The format command with /q performs
options: A low-level format from the factory
A quick format that skips the bad-sector scan
explain: Quick format reinitializes the file system without scanning every sector; full format checks the surface (and on Vista+ zeroes data).

q: Which PowerShell cmdlet tests connectivity to a host and port, succeeding where ping may be blocked?
explain: Test-NetConnection -ComputerName x -Port 443 verifies a specific TCP endpoint even when ICMP is filtered.

q: Get-Service and Start-Service/Stop-Service in PowerShell correspond to which GUI tool?
explain: The *-Service cmdlets manage the same Windows services as the Services console.

q: In PowerShell, Get-EventLog / Get-WinEvent are used to
options: Read Windows event logs from the shell for filtering and scripting
explain: Get-WinEvent queries event logs with filters, enabling automated log review.

q: PowerShell's Get-NetIPAddress and Get-NetAdapter replace much of which legacy tool's role?
options: ipconfig and the Network Connections GUI for viewing adapter configuration
explain: The NetTCPIP/NetAdapter modules expose adapter and IP configuration as objects.

q: To run a PowerShell script downloaded from the internet on one machine for a single session without permanently changing policy, you use
options: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process Bypass (applies only to that session)
explain: Process scope changes last only for the session, the standard safe way to run a one-off script.

q: On Linux, the command to view the running processes in an interactive, updating display is
explain: top shows live process/resource usage; ps gives a static snapshot.

q: 'ps aux' on Linux shows
options: All processes on the system with user, CPU, and memory details
explain: ps aux is the BSD-style listing of every process with resource columns.

q: The Linux command 'kill -9 <pid>' sends
options: SIGKILL, immediately terminating the process without cleanup
explain: -9 (SIGKILL) cannot be caught or ignored; -15 (SIGTERM) is the graceful default.

q: On Linux, 'systemctl status sshd' shows
options: The state and recent log lines of the SSH service unit
explain: systemctl manages systemd units: status, start, stop, enable, restart.

q: To make a Linux service start automatically at boot, you run
explain: enable creates the boot-time links; start only affects the current session.

q: 'df -h' reports
options: Disk space usage of mounted filesystems in human-readable sizes
explain: df shows filesystem capacity/usage; du summarizes directory sizes.

q: 'free -h' on Linux displays
explain: free reports total/used/available memory and swap in readable units.

q: The Linux command to view the last lines of a growing log file in real time is
explain: tail -f follows appended lines; journalctl -f does the same for the systemd journal.

q: 'journalctl -u <unit>' is used to
options: Read the systemd journal entries for a specific service
explain: journalctl filters logs by unit, time, or priority for service troubleshooting.

q: On macOS, the Terminal command 'diskutil list' shows
options: All disks, partitions, and volumes known to the system
explain: diskutil is macOS's disk management CLI; list enumerates devices and APFS containers/volumes.

q: Homebrew on macOS is
options: A third-party package manager for installing command-line tools and apps
explain: brew installs and updates packages on macOS (and Linux) from the shell.

q: On ChromeOS, the crosh shell is opened with
explain: crosh provides basic diagnostics (ping, network tools); a full Linux shell comes from the Linux (Crostini) environment or developer mode.

q: When both NTFS and share permissions apply to a folder accessed over the network, the effective permission is
options: The most restrictive of the two
explain: Network access must pass both layers; the effective result is whichever is more restrictive.

q: An explicit Deny in NTFS permissions generally
options: Is ignored if any Allow exists
Overrides any Allow for the same permission
Applies only to files, not folders
explain: Deny entries take precedence over Allow entries in Windows access checks (explicit deny strongest).

q: A user MOVES a file from one NTFS folder to another folder on the SAME volume. What happens to its permissions?
options: The file keeps its original permissions
It inherits the destination folder's permissions
explain: Moving within the same volume only relocates the file's directory entry, so its ACL travels with it. Copying (or moving across volumes) creates a new file that inherits the destination folder's permissions.

q: A file is COPIED to a different NTFS folder. Its permissions will
options: Stay exactly as they were in the source
Inherit from the new destination folder
explain: Copies are new files and take the destination folder's inheritable permissions.

q: EFS (Encrypting File System) protects files at the level of
options: Individual files/folders, transparently per user account
explain: EFS encrypts per file/folder tied to user keys; BitLocker is the whole-volume solution.

q: What happens if a user encrypts a file with EFS and their profile/keys are lost without a recovery agent or backup certificate?
options: Windows auto-decrypts it at next boot
Any admin can read it anyway
It converts to a zip file
explain: Without the private key or a designated recovery agent, EFS data cannot be decrypted—key backup is essential.

q: NTFS compression and EFS encryption on the same file are
options: Mutually exclusive; a file can be compressed or encrypted, not both
Applied by default to all files
explain: Windows does not allow a file to be both NTFS-compressed and EFS-encrypted at once.

q: Which NTFS permission level lets a user read, write, modify, and delete files but NOT change permissions or take ownership?
explain: Modify is the standard working permission; Full Control adds Change Permissions and Take Ownership.

q: To see who has been accessing a sensitive file, an admin must first
options: Enable Audit Object Access policy, then set auditing on the file; results appear in the Security log
explain: Auditing is two steps: policy enables the category, and the object's SACL defines which access attempts to record.

q: Disk quotas on NTFS volumes are tracked per
explain: Quota entries are per user on each volume; exceeding them can deny further writes (if enforced).

q: Converting a basic disk to dynamic in Disk Management enables
options: Software volumes spanning multiple disks (spanned/striped/mirrored in Windows)
explain: Dynamic disks support multi-disk volumes managed by Windows (largely superseded by Storage Spaces).

q: A mirrored volume in Windows Disk Management/Storage Spaces provides
options: Fault tolerance by duplicating data on two drives
explain: Mirroring (two-way mirror in Storage Spaces) keeps an exact copy on a second drive.

q: A parity layout in Storage Spaces is comparable to
options: RAID 5: capacity-efficient with single-drive fault tolerance
explain: Parity spaces stripe data with parity, surviving one drive failure at write-performance cost.

q: When extending a volume in Disk Management fails because there is no adjacent unallocated space, a common workaround is
options: Use a third-party tool or back up, delete, and recreate the partition layout
explain: Windows extend requires contiguous unallocated space immediately after the volume.

q: Volumes formatted with ReFS are most associated with
options: Servers and Storage Spaces deployments needing high resilience (no chkdsk needed)
explain: ReFS (Resilient File System) targets data volumes/servers with integrity streams; Windows still boots from NTFS.

q: A quick format differs from a full format in that a full format
options: Scans the entire volume for bad sectors (and on modern Windows, zeroes the data)
explain: Full format checks the surface and overwrites data; quick format just reinitializes metadata.

q: FAT32's maximum single-file size is
explain: FAT32 cannot store a file of 4 GB or larger—the classic cause of failed large-file copies to USB drives.

q: exFAT was designed primarily for
options: Flash storage (USB drives/SD cards) needing large-file support without NTFS overhead
explain: exFAT lifts FAT32's file-size limit for removable flash media while staying lightweight.

q: Which file system does macOS use on modern internal drives?
explain: APFS is Apple's current filesystem, optimized for SSDs with snapshots, cloning, and encryption support.

q: A Linux system's standard native filesystem on most distributions today is
explain: ext4 is the default journaling filesystem for most Linux distributions (some use XFS or Btrfs).

q: Defragmenting a traditional hard drive helps performance by
options: Reassembling file fragments contiguously so reads need less head movement
explain: Fragmentation forces the head to seek repeatedly; defrag restores sequential layout on spinning disks.

q: Why does Windows run TRIM optimization instead of defrag on SSDs?
options: SSDs are too fast to defrag
Defragging provides no benefit on flash and shortens SSD life with extra writes
explain: SSDs have no seek penalty; TRIM tells the drive which blocks are free so garbage collection stays efficient.

q: Shadow copies (Previous Versions) allow users to
options: Restore earlier versions of files/folders from automatic restore points
Run a second copy of Windows
explain: Volume Shadow Copy snapshots power the Previous Versions tab for self-service file recovery.

q: A mapped drive created with 'net use' and the /persistent:yes switch will
explain: Persistent mappings are restored at sign-in; non-persistent ones last only for the session.

q: The administrative share C$ is
options: A hidden share of the drive root, accessible to administrators, invisible when browsing
explain: Admin shares (C$, ADMIN$) exist by default for administration and are hidden from network browsing.

q: A UNC path is written in the form
explain: UNC (Universal Naming Convention) addresses network resources as \\server\share.

q: Offline Files (Client-Side Caching) is designed to
options: Keep cached copies of network files available when disconnected, syncing later
explain: CSC lets laptop users work with share contents off-network and reconcile changes on reconnect.

q: When a user encrypts their entire Windows drive with BitLocker, the recovery key should be stored
options: In a text file on the same drive
On a sticky note on the monitor
In Active Directory, a Microsoft account, or a printed/USB copy kept separately
explain: The 48-digit recovery key must be retrievable from somewhere other than the locked disk itself. (BitLocker basics ride the OS domain here; policy detail sits in Security.)

q: Enabling 'Compress this drive to save disk space' on a busy system drive is generally discouraged because
options: It adds CPU overhead to every file operation, slowing the system
explain: Whole-drive NTFS compression trades CPU for space on every read/write—rarely worth it on an OS volume.

q: Ownership of a file (the Owner in advanced security settings) matters because the owner can always
options: Read the file contents regardless of encryption
Change the file's permissions, even if the ACL currently grants them nothing
Delete any other file on the volume
explain: The owner retains the ability to modify the DACL, which is how admins regain control via Take Ownership.

q: A file moved from an NTFS volume to a FAT32 USB drive will lose
options: Its NTFS permissions and alternate data streams (the ACL does not travel to FAT)
explain: FAT32 has no ACL support, so permissions and streams are dropped in the move.

q: Disk Management shows a disk as 'Foreign' after moving it from another Windows machine. The correct action is
options: Import Foreign Disks to bring its dynamic volumes online
explain: Dynamic disks from another machine appear as Foreign; importing preserves their volumes (initializing would wipe them).

q: A GPT disk is required instead of MBR when
options: Booting Windows in UEFI mode, or using drives larger than 2 TB
explain: MBR caps at 2 TB and 4 primary partitions; UEFI Windows installs require GPT.

q: The EFI System Partition (ESP) contains
options: The boot loaders and boot applications the UEFI firmware launches
explain: UEFI firmware loads boot entries (e.g., Windows Boot Manager) from the FAT32 ESP.

q: Extending a striped volume's performance benefit comes at the cost of
options: Higher failure risk: if any member disk fails, the whole volume's data is lost
explain: Striping (RAID 0 style) spreads data so one disk failure destroys the set.

q: To audit which files a departing employee copied, the most OS-native source is
options: The Security event log, provided object-access auditing was enabled beforehand
explain: Without auditing enabled in advance, Windows keeps no per-file access history—forensics then need other tools.

q: Folder Redirection in a domain environment moves
options: Known folders (Documents, Desktop) to a server location while appearing local to the user
Local user profiles into the cloud
explain: Redirected folders centralize user data for backup while keeping the familiar paths.

q: A user's profile fails to load and Windows signs them in with a temporary profile. A common fix is
options: Repair or recreate the user profile (back up data, delete the corrupt profile entry, sign in fresh)
explain: Temp profiles stem from profile corruption or a locked .bak registry entry; recreating the profile resolves it.

q: The NTUSER.DAT file in a profile stores
options: That user's registry hive (loaded as HKEY_CURRENT_USER at sign-in)
explain: Each profile's NTUSER.DAT becomes HKCU when the user logs on; corruption breaks user settings.

q: A roaming profile differs from a local profile in that it
options: Is stored on a server and follows the user between domain computers
explain: Roaming profiles copy down at logon and back at logoff from a network share.

q: Mandatory profiles are used when
options: Users must get an identical, non-persistent desktop (changes are discarded at logoff)
explain: Mandatory profiles enforce a fixed environment—common in labs and kiosks.

q: In Linux, the section of the filesystem where user home directories live is
explain: Standard users get /home/<username>; root's home is /root.

q: On Linux, 'chmod 750' on a file grants
options: Owner: read/write/execute; group: read/execute; others: no access
explain: Octal digits sum read(4)+write(2)+execute(1) per class: 7=rwx, 5=r-x, 0=none.

q: The Linux 'chown' command changes
explain: chown sets ownership; chmod sets permission bits; umask sets defaults for new files.

q: On macOS, Time Machine backs up to the chosen disk using which filesystem imaging approach?
options: Full disk clones every hour only
Zip archives of the home folder
APFS snapshots on modern macOS for local snapshots plus incremental backups to the destination
explain: Modern Time Machine leverages APFS snapshots, keeping hourly/daily/weekly incremental versions.

q: A standard user account differs from an administrator account in that a standard user cannot
options: Save files to their own profile
Install software for all users or change system-wide settings without elevation credentials
explain: Standard users work in their own scope; system changes require an admin's credentials via UAC.

q: When joining a PC to a domain, which of these is a prerequisite?
options: The user must have a Microsoft account with a credit card
The PC must be formatted first
The PC must have a Pro, Enterprise, or Education edition of Windows and be able to reach a domain controller
The PC must have two hard drives
explain: Windows Home cannot join domains; DNS must resolve the domain and a DC must be reachable.

q: A workstation cannot contact the domain at logon after a network change; users see 'The trust relationship between this workstation and the primary domain failed.' A common cause/fix pair is
options: Cause: the monitor is asleep; Fix: reboot the DC
Cause: the machine account password is out of sync; Fix: reset the machine account or rejoin the domain
Cause: the user's password expired; Fix: buy a new PC
Cause: DNS is fine; Fix: ignore it
explain: Workstations authenticate with their own machine-account password; when it desyncs from AD, trust fails until reset/repaired (e.g., Test-ComputerSecureChannel -Repair or rejoin).

q: A workgroup differs from a domain in that a workgroup
options: Has no central directory; each PC manages its own accounts
explain: Workgroups are peer-to-peer with per-machine SAM databases—no centralized authentication or policy.

q: The format user@domain.com used in logons is called a
explain: UPNs look like email addresses and are the modern domain logon format.

q: Group Policy objects are applied in which order?
options: Local, then Site, then Domain, then OU (LSDOU), with the last applied winning conflicts
explain: LSDOU: later (closer) policies override earlier ones for the same setting unless blocked/enforced.

q: A GPO marked 'Enforced' (No Override) means
options: Its settings cannot be overridden by later GPOs or blocked by OU admins
It disables inheritance for the whole domain
explain: Enforced GPOs win conflicts even against child OUs that block inheritance.

q: 'Block Inheritance' on an OU stops
options: GPOs from parent containers applying to that OU (except Enforced ones)
explain: Blocking inheritance filters parent GPOs; Enforced GPOs still apply by design.

q: Loopback processing in Group Policy is used so that
options: User settings from the computer's location apply (e.g., kiosk machines) regardless of who logs on
explain: Loopback (merge or replace) makes the machine's OU user-side settings govern—classic for kiosks and RDS hosts.

q: The default background Group Policy refresh interval for domain workstations is about
options: 90 minutes (with a random offset up to 30 minutes)
explain: Background refresh occurs roughly every 90±30 minutes for computers and users.

q: An account lockout threshold of 5 with a 30-minute duration means
options: After 5 bad attempts the account locks for 30 minutes (or until an admin unlocks it)
The account is deleted after 5 tries
explain: Lockout policy balances brute-force resistance against denial-of-service from accidental lockouts.

q: Setting minimum password length and complexity requirements is done in
options: Password Policy (Account Policies) in Group Policy or local security policy
explain: Password Policy lives under Account Policies; fine-grained policies (PSOs) can target specific groups in AD.

q: A password that never expires for a service account should instead be managed as
options: A shared password in a spreadsheet
The same password as the domain admin
A group Managed Service Account (gMSA) so AD rotates the password automatically
explain: gMSAs eliminate manual service-account password management with automatic 30-day rotation.

q: Local Security Policy (secpol.msc) configures, among other things
options: Audit policy, user rights assignment, and security options on a single machine
explain: secpol is the local subset of security settings; domain settings come from GPOs.

q: Which audit category must be enabled to log successful and failed logon attempts?
options: Audit Logon Events (or Advanced Audit: Logon/Logoff)
explain: Logon auditing writes 4624/4625 events to the Security log—foundational for security monitoring.

q: Securing the sign-in screen, Windows Hello PIN is considered safer than a password in one key way:
options: The PIN is tied to that specific device (backed by TPM) and never travels to a server
The PIN works on any computer
explain: A Hello PIN unlocks device-bound keys; stealing it alone is useless without the physical device.

q: Dynamic Lock automatically locks a PC when
options: The user's paired Bluetooth phone moves out of range
explain: Dynamic Lock uses Bluetooth proximity as a walk-away signal.

q: Windows licenses for a PC built with an OEM key differ from retail in that OEM licenses
options: Are tied to the first motherboard and are not transferable to a new PC
explain: OEM licenses live and die with the original hardware; retail licenses can move between the user's PCs.

q: KMS activation in an enterprise requires
options: Each PC to call Microsoft individually
A KMS host on the network that clients contact; activation lasts 180 days and renews automatically
Internet access for every activation forever
explain: Key Management Service activates volume clients locally; they must renew against the host at least every 180 days.

q: MAK activation differs from KMS in that MAK
options: Activates each machine directly with Microsoft using a key with a set number of activations
Never needs activation again after imaging
explain: Multiple Activation Keys suit smaller or disconnected environments where a KMS host is not justified.

q: The slmgr.vbs command is used to
options: Manage Windows licensing: view activation status (/dli, /xpr) and install keys (/ipk)
explain: Software License Manager scripts handle key installation, activation, and status checks.

q: A digital license (digital entitlement) activates Windows by
options: Storing the key on the hard drive
Requiring a sticker on the case
Linking the hardware ID to Microsoft's servers (optionally tied to a Microsoft account for transfers)
Needing a phone call each boot
explain: Digital licenses activate automatically when the same hardware contacts Microsoft; linking to an MS account eases reactivation after hardware changes.

q: Upgrading Windows 10 Home to Pro in place is typically done by
options: Entering a Pro product key in Settings > Activation (or buying the upgrade in the Store)
explain: Edition upgrades are a key change plus feature unlock—files and apps stay in place.

q: Downgrade rights matter to businesses because they allow
options: Running an earlier Windows version under a newer version's license (per Microsoft's terms)
explain: Certain volume/OEM licenses permit installing a previous version until the organization is ready to migrate.

q: An evaluation copy of Windows Server/Enterprise will eventually
options: Expire and begin shutting down or nagging until activated with a full license
explain: Eval builds have fixed lifetimes (often 180 days) after which they enforce activation.

q: When a user signs in with a Microsoft account, which benefit is OS-integrated?
options: Settings, passwords, and preferences roam between their Windows devices via sync
explain: Microsoft-account sync roams personalization, Wi-Fi, and credential data across the user's PCs.

q: OneDrive Files On-Demand (Files Online) saves local disk space by
options: Showing placeholders and downloading files only when opened
Storing everything in the Recycle Bin
explain: Online-only files appear in Explorer but fetch on first use; 'Always keep on this device' pins them locally.

q: A folder shown with a cloud icon overlay in Explorer is
options: An online-only OneDrive file not yet downloaded
explain: The cloud badge marks placeholder files in OneDrive's on-demand system; a green check means locally available.

q: To prevent a PC from joining a workgroup's shared media streaming, and to harden it on public networks, you set the network profile to
options: Public, which enables stricter firewall rules and disables discovery
explain: Public profile treats the network as untrusted: discovery and sharing are off by default.

q: Network discovery and file sharing work out of the box when the profile is set to
explain: Private profiles enable discovery/sharing services intended for home and office LANs.

q: Windows' 'Require sign-in: when PC wakes from sleep' option is found under
explain: Sign-in options centralize password/PIN/Hello requirements, wake behavior, and dynamic lock.

q: Fast User Switching allows
options: Multiple users to stay signed in with apps running while another user works
explain: Switching keeps sessions alive in memory—convenient, at the cost of RAM and unsaved-work risk when shutting down.

q: 'Run as administrator' differs from 'Run as different user' in that it
options: Skips the UAC prompt in all cases
Elevates the current user's token (or prompts for admin credentials), while 'different user' starts the app under another account entirely
explain: Shift-right-click exposes 'Run as different user' for launching apps (like admin tools) under alternate credentials.

q: Parental controls in Windows (Microsoft Family Safety) can enforce
options: Screen time limits, content filters, and activity reports for child accounts
explain: Family Safety manages child Microsoft accounts across Windows, Xbox, and Android.

q: Which Windows edition supports joining a domain, Group Policy, and BitLocker out of the box, targeting small businesses?
explain: Pro is the business baseline: domain join, gpedit, BitLocker, Remote Desktop host, Hyper-V.

q: Remote Desktop (as a host) is supported natively on which editions?
options: Pro, Enterprise, and Education (Home can only be a client)
No editions; it is a paid add-on
explain: Home includes the Remote Desktop client but cannot accept incoming RDP sessions.

q: Hyper-V as a Windows feature is available on
options: Pro, Enterprise, and Education editions (64-bit with SLAT)
explain: Hyper-V requires a higher edition plus hardware virtualization support (SLAT).

q: Windows in S mode restricts the system to
options: Apps from the Microsoft Store only, for security and performance
explain: S mode locks app installation to the Store; switching out is one-way and free.

q: To see exactly which Windows edition, version, and build a PC runs for compatibility checks, the fastest one-stop tool is
options: Settings > System > About (or winver for version/build)
explain: About lists edition, version, build, and system type in one screen.

q: In a domain, time synchronization matters to Kerberos because tickets are rejected when clock skew exceeds
explain: Domain members sync from the PDC emulator; skew beyond the tolerance fails authentication.

q: A security baseline applied via GPO commonly disables
options: SMBv1, LLMNR/NetBIOS where unused, and restricts local admin membership
explain: Baselines remove legacy protocols and tighten admin rights; Microsoft publishes ready-made baseline GPOs.

q: When a departing employee's account must be preserved for investigation but unusable, the admin should
options: Rename it to the new hire
Disable the account (not delete it), preserving its SID, group memberships, and audit trail
explain: Disabling preserves evidence and ownership history; deletion destroys the SID link to files and logs.

q: Cached domain credentials let a laptop user
options: Sign in with their domain account while away from the network (a limited number of cached logons)
explain: Windows caches a verifier of recent domain logons so travel does not lock users out; it does not store the plain password.

q: A local account password reset disk works only
options: For that specific local account and must have been created before the password was forgotten
explain: Password reset disks are per-account USB keys for local accounts; Microsoft accounts reset online.

q: Forgot a Microsoft account password at the Windows sign-in screen—the user should
options: Reset it online from another device (or the 'I forgot my password' link if shown); the PC updates when back online
explain: Cloud account credentials are recovered through Microsoft's online flow, not local tools.

q: The two fundamental Windows installation types from setup media are
explain: Setup offers Upgrade to preserve the environment, or Custom for a fresh installation to a chosen partition.

q: Before an in-place upgrade, the most important preparation is
options: A verified backup/image of the system and data
explain: Even reliable upgrades can fail; a restorable image is the rollback plan.

q: Which tool from Microsoft creates bootable Windows installation USB media and downloads the latest image?
explain: Microsoft's Media Creation Tool builds current installation media and can perform in-place upgrades.

q: UEFI systems require Windows installation media's boot partition to be formatted as
options: FAT32 for the EFI System Partition
explain: UEFI firmware reads FAT32 ESPs; installers place boot files there even when the OS volume is NTFS.

q: Windows 11's official minimum hardware requirements include
options: TPM 2.0, Secure Boot-capable UEFI firmware, and a supported CPU
explain: TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot are the headline Windows 11 gates; PC Health Check validates a machine.

q: Sysprep's purpose in image deployment is to
options: Generalize a Windows installation (removing unique SIDs/settings) so it can be captured and deployed to many machines
explain: Sysprep /generalize prepares a reference PC for imaging without duplicating machine-specific identity.

q: An unattend answer file (autounattend.xml) lets an installer
options: Automate Windows Setup choices (locale, partitions, keys) for hands-free deployment
explain: Answer files feed Setup its answers during specialize/oobeSystem passes—standard in enterprise imaging.

q: WDS (Windows Deployment Services) provides
explain: WDS lets clients boot from the network and pull down captured images—MDT/Intune extend the model.

q: A difference between a 'feature update' and a 'quality update' in Windows Update is
options: Feature updates deliver a new Windows version/build annually; quality updates are monthly security and reliability fixes
explain: Feature updates = new build cadence; quality updates = cumulative monthly servicing.

q: After a feature update, Windows keeps the previous installation for rollback for how long by default?
explain: The rollback window defaults to 10 days; Storage Sense/Disk Cleanup can remove Windows.old earlier.

q: To uninstall a problematic quality update, an admin can use
options: Settings > Windows Update > Update history > Uninstall updates (or wusa /uninstall)
explain: Update history offers uninstall for most quality updates; WinRE can remove packages offline with DISM.

q: Windows Update repeatedly fails with corruption errors despite restarts. A deeper repair sequence is
options: Stop the update services, rename SoftwareDistribution (and catroot2), restart services; then DISM/SFC if needed
explain: Resetting the download cache/components is the standard escalation before image repair.

q: The Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) can be reached by
options: Holding Shift while choosing Restart, via Settings > Recovery, or automatically after repeated boot failures
Pressing F12 only on Dell machines
Unplugging the PC three times only
Safe Mode is the only way
explain: Shift+Restart and Settings > System > Recovery > Advanced startup both boot into WinRE.

q: Windows virtual desktops (Task View) are used to
options: Run multiple copies of Windows at once
Organize open apps into separate workspaces (e.g., one for email/admin, one for a project) that can be switched with Win+Tab or Ctrl+Win+arrow
explain: Virtual desktops are a window-management feature—not virtual machines; apps keep running across desktops.

q: System Restore in WinRE differs from System Image Recovery in that System Restore
options: Rolls back system files, registry, and drivers to a restore point without touching personal files
explain: Restore points are lightweight system-state snapshots; image recovery is a full-volume restore.

q: If a PC blue-screens after a driver update, the fastest recovery inside WinRE's Startup Settings is
options: Boot into Safe Mode and roll back or uninstall the driver
Run Memory Diagnostics for a day
explain: Safe Mode loads minimal drivers, letting you remove the offending driver package.

q: Disable Driver Signature Enforcement from Startup Settings is used when
options: Installing a legitimate legacy/test driver that is not signed, for that boot only
explain: The setting lasts one boot and exists for legacy hardware—permanently disabling signature checks is a security risk.

q: To access a command prompt for offline repairs on a PC that will not boot, you use
options: The sign-in screen's Ease of Access button only
WinRE > Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Command Prompt
explain: WinRE's command prompt runs offline against the installed Windows (drive letters may shift).

q: In WinRE's command prompt, the installed Windows volume often appears as a different drive letter because
options: WinRE assigns letters in its own order; verify with diskpart 'list volume' before running repairs
explain: Technicians confirm the real Windows path (dir D:\Windows) before DISM/SFC offline switches.

q: Running SFC against an offline Windows installation requires the form
options: Plain sfc /scannow in WinRE works automatically
explain: Offline SFC needs explicit boot and Windows directories because it is not running inside the target OS.

q: DISM can service an offline image using
explain: The /Image switch points DISM at a mounted or offline Windows directory instead of the running OS.

q: A recovery drive (USB) created from a working Windows PC can
options: Boot a non-booting PC into WinRE and, if it includes system files, reinstall Windows
explain: Recovery USBs are bootable repair media; including system files adds a bare-metal reinstall option.

q: 'Reset this PC > Remove everything > Cloud download' is the best choice when
options: The user wants to keep all apps
There is no internet and no media
The local recovery image may be corrupt and a completely clean Windows is desired
explain: Cloud download fetches a pristine image from Microsoft, bypassing damaged local recovery files.

q: BitLocker-protected drives in WinRE will prompt for
options: The 48-digit recovery key before the volume can be unlocked for repairs
explain: WinRE cannot read an encrypted volume until it is unlocked with the recovery key.

q: A PC fails to boot after RAM is upgraded and beeps/loops before POST completes. The Windows-side recovery tools are irrelevant because
options: The failure is at hardware/POST level, before any OS or recovery environment loads
explain: No-POST faults are hardware/firmware problems; OS recovery starts only after firmware hands off.

q: When Windows Setup reports 'Windows cannot be installed to this disk' on a UEFI system because the disk is MBR, the installer-side fix is
options: Delete the partitions and let Setup create a GPT layout (data loss) or convert the disk with a tool first
explain: UEFI mode requires GPT; Setup can reinitialize an empty disk to GPT during a custom install.

q: MBR2GPT is a Microsoft tool that
options: Converts a Windows disk from MBR to GPT in place without data loss (when validation passes)
explain: mbr2gpt /validate then /convert migrates BIOS installs to UEFI/GPT without wiping.

q: An upgrade from Windows 10 to Windows 11 keeps
options: Nothing; it is always a clean install
Files, settings, and compatible applications when done as an in-place upgrade via Setup/Windows Update
Only files in the Recycle Bin
explain: In-place upgrades preserve the user environment; unsupported hardware blocks the offer.

q: If Windows Update says a PC 'doesn't currently meet the requirements' for Windows 11, the technician should
options: Run PC Health Check to identify the specific blocker (TPM, Secure Boot, CPU) and address it in firmware if supported
Install Windows 11 anyway with registry hacks as the first resort
Tell the user to buy a new PC immediately
explain: Most blockers are firmware settings (TPM/fTPM or Secure Boot toggles) rather than true hardware absence.

q: The 'Windows.old' folder contains
options: The previous Windows installation kept for rollback and manual file recovery after an upgrade
explain: Windows.old holds the prior OS tree (~10 days) and is a source for rescuing files after bad upgrades.

q: Safe Mode with Networking differs from plain Safe Mode by
options: Also loading network drivers/services so the user can download tools or reach shares
explain: Networking variant adds NIC drivers and related services—useful but riskier during malware cleanup.

q: Safe Mode with Command Prompt boots to
options: A minimal environment that opens a command window instead of the Explorer shell
explain: It is the fallback when Explorer itself crashes on logon.

q: VGA/low-resolution mode historically, and 'Enable low-resolution video' in Startup Settings, helps when
options: A bad display setting or driver leaves the screen unreadable at native settings
explain: Low-res video loads a basic display path so the correct driver/settings can be restored.

q: Automatic Repair loops (preparing automatic repair, then failing) most often indicate
options: Corrupt boot/startup components or a failing disk; investigate via WinRE tools and disk health checks
explain: Boot loops point at BCD/startup corruption or hardware (disk) problems—diagnose from WinRE, not repeated restarts.

q: A PC upgraded to a new motherboard will usually need Windows reactivation because
options: The digital license is tied to the previous hardware ID (motherboard)
explain: Significant hardware changes (motherboard) change the hardware hash; linking the license to a Microsoft account enables the Activation troubleshooter transfer.

q: OOBE is the phase of setup where
options: The user creates the first account and chooses privacy/region settings (Out-Of-Box Experience)
explain: OOBE is the first-run experience after installation completes.

q: Choosing 'I don't have internet' / offline setup historically allowed creating
options: A local account instead of a Microsoft account during OOBE (options vary by version)
An admin account with no password required
explain: Home editions push Microsoft accounts; offline paths (where offered) create local accounts—enterprises use deployment tools instead.

q: Windows installation from an ISO mounted in File Explorer is suitable for
options: Bare-metal installs on an empty disk (without other media)
In-place upgrades or repairs launched from within a running Windows
explain: Mounting the ISO and running setup.exe is the classic in-place upgrade/repair path.

q: Before deploying an image to 500 identical laptops, the reference machine should be
options: Activated with a retail key and left running
Joined to the domain as a user PC
Sysprepped (generalized) and shut down, then captured
explain: Generalize removes unique identifiers so each deployment generates fresh SIDs and setup passes.

q: Windows activation after imaging with a volume license is typically handled by
options: KMS or Active Directory-Based Activation automatically when the machines join the network/domain
Typing the same retail key everywhere
explain: Volume images carry a generic KMS client key; activation happens automatically against the org's infrastructure.

q: An 'in-place upgrade repair' (repair install) is chosen to
options: Fix deep Windows corruption while keeping files, settings, and installed apps
explain: Running Setup over the existing install refreshes system files without an app/data wipe—the last step before clean install.

q: To create a bootable installer from an ISO using only built-in Windows tools on a UEFI machine, a technician can
options: Copy the ISO file alone onto an NTFS USB in all cases
Format USB as FAT32 and copy the ISO's contents onto it (splitting install.wim if over 4 GB)
explain: UEFI can boot a FAT32 USB with extracted setup files; the 4 GB FAT32 limit is why large install.wim files need DISM splitting.

q: A dual-boot system chooses the default OS and menu timeout through
options: System Properties > Startup and Recovery, msconfig's Boot tab, or bcdedit
explain: BCD settings govern the boot menu; GUI and CLI tools both edit it.

q: When the boot menu shows two entries both named 'Windows 11' after an upgrade, the extra entry usually points to
options: A leftover or second installation (e.g., Windows.old-era BCD entry or a second volume) that can be removed with msconfig/bcdedit after verifying
explain: Stale BCD entries are common after in-place work; verify which volume each entry boots before deleting.

q: Recovery partitions should generally not be deleted casually because they
options: Hold the WinRE tools needed for resets and repairs; removing them breaks recovery options
Speed up the PC when deleted
explain: Deleting the recovery partition removes built-in WinRE/reset capability; it can be rebuilt but with effort.

q: macOS Finder is the equivalent of which Windows component?
explain: Finder is the Mac's file manager and desktop shell, like Explorer on Windows.

q: Mission Control on macOS provides
options: An overview of all open windows, desktops (Spaces), and full-screen apps
explain: Mission Control (F3/three-finger swipe) exposes Spaces and windows for navigation.

q: Spotlight is used on macOS to
options: Search files, apps, and information across the Mac (Cmd+Space)
explain: Spotlight is the system-wide search; it also does calculations and definitions.

q: Gatekeeper on macOS enforces
options: Which sources apps may be installed from (App Store / identified developers) and first-launch checks
explain: Gatekeeper verifies code signatures/notarization when apps are first opened.

q: Rosetta 2 on Apple silicon Macs allows
options: Apps built for Intel Macs to run via translation
iOS apps to be sideloaded only
explain: Rosetta 2 translates x86-64 code to ARM at install/first run with minor performance cost.

q: Boot Camp historically allowed Intel Macs to
options: Dual-boot Windows natively (not available on Apple silicon)
explain: Boot Camp Assistant partitions the drive and supports a native Windows install on Intel Macs only.

q: macOS Recovery on an Apple silicon Mac is entered by
options: Holding the power button at startup until startup options appear, then choosing Options
explain: Apple silicon uses the power-button startup options screen; Intel Macs use Cmd+R and variants.

q: Disk Utility's First Aid does what for a Mac volume?
options: Checks and repairs filesystem errors (like chkdsk's role)
explain: First Aid verifies/repairs directory structures on HFS+/APFS volumes.

q: Keychain Access on macOS stores
options: Passwords, certificates, and secure notes for the user
explain: Keychains hold login credentials and certs; the login keychain unlocks with the account password.

q: FileVault on macOS is
options: Full-disk encryption for the startup disk
explain: FileVault 2 encrypts the entire startup volume with XTS-AES, unlocked at pre-boot by authorized users/recovery key.

q: To force-quit an unresponsive Mac app, you use
options: Command+Option+Esc to open the Force Quit window
explain: Force Quit is the Mac equivalent of ending a hung task.

q: A Mac boots to a flashing question-mark folder icon. This indicates
options: No bootable system was found (drive/Startup Disk problem)
explain: The question mark means firmware could not find a valid startup volume—disk or OS damage.

q: The macOS equivalent of Task Manager for killing processes is
explain: Activity Monitor shows processes/resources and can force-quit them; Console reads logs.

q: Linux 'sudo' is used to
options: Run a command with elevated (root) privileges after authenticating
explain: sudo grants temporary root rights per command; su switches the whole shell.

q: A Linux package manager such as apt or dnf handles
options: Installing, updating, and removing software packages along with their dependencies
explain: Package managers resolve dependencies from repositories and track installed software.

q: 'apt update' differs from 'apt upgrade' in that 'update'
options: Only refreshes the package lists; 'upgrade' actually installs newer versions
explain: The two-step update-then-upgrade flow is a classic Linux exam distinction.

q: The '~' symbol in a Linux shell refers to
explain: Tilde expands to $HOME; '/' is root, '..' is parent, '.' is current.

q: In Linux paths, '/etc' primarily holds
explain: /etc is the configuration directory; /var holds logs/spool, /tmp is temporary.

q: 'grep' is used to
options: Search text within files or piped output for matching patterns
explain: grep filters lines by pattern—central to log analysis pipelines.

q: The 'man' command provides
options: Manual pages documenting commands and their options
explain: man <command> opens the reference documentation installed with the system.

q: 'tar' is primarily used to
options: Create and extract archive files (often combined with gzip as .tar.gz)
explain: tar bundles files into archives; compression is added via gzip/bzip2/xz flags.

q: A Linux file with permissions 'rwxr-xr--' allows the owner to
options: Read, write, and execute; group can read/execute; others can only read
explain: Read the triplets left to right: owner rwx, group r-x, others r--.

q: ChromeOS devices are managed at scale through
options: The Google Admin console (Chrome management policies)
explain: Admin console policies control Chromebooks fleet-wide: apps, extensions, updates, restrictions.

q: ChromeOS updates are delivered
options: Automatically in the background with a dual-partition (A/B) design, applied at reboot
Manually by each user downloading installers
explain: ChromeOS keeps two system partitions so updates install to the idle one and swap at restart—seamless and rollback-capable.

q: The Linux environment on Chromebooks (Crostini) runs Linux apps
options: Inside a container within a virtual machine, isolated from ChromeOS
With full access to the host kernel settings
explain: Crostini's VM (Termina) + container model keeps Linux apps sandboxed from the verified OS.

q: A Chromebook 'powerwash' that a user can start from Settings is blocked on managed devices when
options: Admin policy disables factory reset for enrolled devices
The device is in tablet mode
explain: Enterprise enrollment can prohibit powerwash to keep devices managed.

q: Verified boot on ChromeOS protects the OS by
options: Requiring a password at every boot
Checking firmware/OS integrity at startup and restoring from the known-good copy if tampered
explain: Verified (secure) boot plus A/B partitions lets ChromeOS self-heal a compromised system image.

q: Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) lets Windows users
options: Boot Linux instead of Windows permanently
Run a genuine Linux environment and command-line tools directly on Windows
explain: WSL 2 uses a lightweight VM with a real Linux kernel; distributions install from the Store.

q: To see the Windows build's installed optional features such as Telnet Client or .NET 3.5, you open
explain: Windows Features toggles components like .NET Framework 3.5, Hyper-V, and WSL.

q: .NET Framework 3.5 installation fails online on some PCs because it must be
options: Sourced from Windows Update or installation media (DISM with /Source) as a feature on demand
explain: .NET 3.5 is a Feature on Demand; offline environments need media as the source.

q: Windows 'God Mode' is an informal name for
options: A folder shortcut ({ED7BA470...}) that lists all Control Panel tasks in one view
explain: The 'All Tasks' shell folder aggregates every control setting; it's a convenience, not a privilege escalation.

q: The Reliability Monitor (perfmon /rel) is useful because it
options: Shows a timeline of application crashes, Windows failures, and updates to correlate when problems began
explain: Reliability history visually ties instability to installs/updates—a fast triage view.

q: Windows Memory Diagnostic tests
options: System RAM for errors (runs at reboot, outside Windows)
explain: mdsched schedules a boot-time RAM test; results appear in Event Viewer after logon.

q: A PC suspected of RAM errors should also be tested with the understanding that
options: Intermittent errors may need extended/multiple passes to surface
Errors only occur in Safe Mode
explain: Marginal RAM can pass short tests; overnight MemTest86-style runs catch heat/timing-related faults.

q: The 'sxstrace' and SideBySide errors in Event Viewer relate to
options: Visual C++ runtime/assembly conflicts for older applications
explain: SxS errors mean an app requested a runtime version that is missing or corrupt; installing the right VC++ redistributable fixes it.

q: Compatibility Mode for a legacy application can emulate
options: Earlier Windows versions' behaviors plus settings like reduced color mode and DPI scaling overrides
explain: The Compatibility tab (and Program Compatibility Troubleshooter) applies shims for old apps.

q: High-DPI scaling problems (blurry legacy apps) are addressed via
options: Lowering the monitor's native resolution permanently
The app's Compatibility settings: override DPI scaling behavior (System/Application)
explain: Per-app DPI awareness overrides fix blurry or mis-sized legacy windows on high-resolution displays.

q: Windows' built-in screen recording for apps (Win+G) comes from
explain: Game Bar records app windows and captures clips/screenshots—useful for documenting repro steps.

q: Sticky Keys, Filter Keys, and Toggle Keys are examples of
explain: These assist users with motor impairments; accidentally triggering Sticky Keys (Shift x5) is a classic help-desk call.

q: Narrator and Magnifier serve users who need
options: Screen reading (text-to-speech) and screen magnification for low vision
explain: Narrator reads the UI aloud; Magnifier enlarges portions of the screen.

q: The three classic authentication factor categories are
options: Something you know, something you type, something you see
Something you know, something you have, and something you are
explain: Knowledge, possession, and inherence are the factor families; two factors from the SAME family (password + PIN) are not true MFA.

q: A time-based one-time password (TOTP) authenticator app works by
options: Generating codes from a shared secret and the current time, rotating every 30 seconds
explain: TOTP codes derive from a seed plus time steps, which is why device clock accuracy matters.

q: Passkeys (FIDO2/WebAuthn) improve on passwords mainly because they are
options: Phishing-resistant: the credential is bound to the legitimate site's origin
explain: With passkeys the private key never leaves the authenticator and the challenge is origin-bound, defeating look-alike phishing sites.

q: Kerberos authentication issues a user a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) after initial logon so they can
options: Request service tickets for resources without re-entering credentials
explain: The TGT proves authentication to the KDC, which then issues per-service tickets (SSO in AD).

q: SAML and OpenID Connect are primarily used for
options: Federated single sign-on between identity providers and applications
explain: Federation lets one IdP authenticate users to many apps; SAML is XML-based enterprise SSO, OIDC is the OAuth2-based modern standard.

q: RADIUS and TACACS+ differ in that TACACS+
options: Uses TCP and encrypts the entire payload; RADIUS uses UDP and encrypts only the password
explain: TACACS+ (Cisco) separates AAA functions and fully encrypts; RADIUS combines auth/accounting over UDP.

q: Port security on a switch with 'sticky' MAC learning does what?
options: Learns and saves the MAC addresses allowed on a port and can shut the port down on a violation
Encrypts all traffic on the port
explain: Sticky port security binds a port to known devices to prevent unauthorized swaps and rogue connections.

q: DHCP snooping protects a LAN by
options: Blocking rogue DHCP servers from answering on untrusted ports
explain: Snooping builds a binding table of legitimate leases and drops DHCP offers from untrusted ports.

q: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) prevents ARP spoofing by
options: Validating ARP packets against the DHCP snooping binding table
Assigning static IPs to servers only
explain: DAI checks that ARP claims match known IP-MAC bindings, blunting MITM via ARP poisoning.

q: The three roles in an 802.1X deployment are
explain: The authenticator passes EAP messages between the supplicant and the RADIUS server until access is granted.

q: EAP-TLS is considered the strongest common EAP method because
options: Both the client and server authenticate with certificates (mutual authentication)
It is the fastest to deploy
explain: Mutual certificate authentication removes password-based weaknesses; deployment cost is the trade-off.

q: Network Access Control (NAC) posture assessment might check a connecting device for
options: Current patches, antivirus status, disk encryption, and a healthy firewall before granting access
explain: NAC enforces endpoint health policies, quarantining non-compliant devices to a remediation VLAN.

q: Credential stuffing attacks succeed because of
options: Weak encryption on the target site
Users reusing the same password across many sites, letting breached credentials unlock other accounts
explain: Attackers replay breached username/password pairs at scale; unique passwords and MFA defeat it.

q: The principle of least privilege means
options: Users and processes get only the minimum access required for their tasks
Everyone gets read access to everything
explain: Least privilege limits the blast radius of mistakes and compromised accounts.

q: Just-in-time (JIT) privileged access improves security by
options: Granting admin rights only when needed and for a limited time, instead of standing privileges
explain: JIT elevation through PAM tools shrinks the window in which powerful rights exist to be abused.

q: Windows LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) protects against lateral movement by
options: Disabling the local admin account's password entirely
Using the same password on all PCs
Removing local admin accounts from the OS
Randomizing and centrally managing a unique local admin password on every machine
explain: Unique per-machine passwords stop attackers from using one cracked local admin password everywhere (pass-the-hash).

q: Credential Guard on Windows protects secrets by
options: Storing passwords in a text file
Isolating LSASS credential material inside a virtualization-based secure enclave
explain: VBS-based isolation keeps hashes/tickets out of the normal OS memory that tools like Mimikatz scrape.

q: Controlled Folder Access in Windows Security helps stop ransomware by
options: Blocking untrusted apps from writing to protected folders such as Documents
explain: CFA guards user folders against mass modification by unknown processes.

q: Memory integrity (HVCI / core isolation) enforces
options: Kernel code integrity using virtualization-based security, blocking unsigned kernel code
explain: HVCI ensures only trusted code runs in kernel mode, a key defense against malicious drivers.

q: BitLocker with TPM+PIN is stronger than TPM-only because
options: It works without a TPM chip
It adds a knowledge factor at pre-boot, so a stolen powered-off machine cannot auto-unlock just by having the TPM
explain: TPM-only transparently unseals for anyone who boots the machine; a PIN stops offline attacks on stolen hardware.

q: BitLocker To Go applies to
options: Removable drives (USB sticks and external drives)
explain: BitLocker To Go encrypts removable media, prompting for a password on other machines.

q: A salted, slow hashing algorithm such as bcrypt is used for storing passwords because
options: Salts defeat rainbow tables and the slowness makes brute force expensive
explain: Passwords are hashed (one-way), never encrypted for verification; salts are unique per password.

q: In PKI, a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) is
options: A request containing a public key and identity info, sent to a CA to be signed into a certificate
explain: The CA validates identity and signs the CSR, producing the certificate; the private key never leaves the requester.

q: A wildcard certificate for *.example.com covers
options: All first-level subdomains of example.com (such as mail.example.com)
explain: Wildcards match one label deep—convenient, but a compromised key affects every covered host.

q: The main risk of self-signed certificates on internal sites is
options: Users are trained to click through trust warnings, and there's no third-party identity validation
explain: Self-signed certs encrypt fine but provide no chain of trust, normalizing warning click-through.

q: Certificate revocation status is checked via
options: CRL (revocation lists) or OCSP (online status queries)
explain: OCSP gives real-time status; CRLs are periodically published signed lists; stapling speeds OCSP delivery.

q: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated mainly because
options: They rely on weak cryptographic algorithms and are vulnerable to known attacks
explain: Modern standards (PCI DSS etc.) require TLS 1.2+; legacy protocols enable downgrade and crypto attacks.

q: Symmetric encryption is used for bulk data (and asymmetric for key exchange) because
options: Asymmetric encryption cannot encrypt data at all
Symmetric algorithms are far faster; asymmetric math securely establishes the shared key
explain: Hybrid design: RSA/ECDH exchanges or wraps a session key, then AES encrypts the traffic.

q: A digital signature on an email or document provides
options: Authentication of the sender and integrity of the content (and non-repudiation)
explain: Signing hashes and encrypts the hash with the private key; anyone can verify with the public key, but content stays readable unless also encrypted.

q: S/MIME is used to
options: Sign and encrypt email messages using certificates
explain: S/MIME provides end-to-end message signing/encryption based on X.509 certificates.

q: A hardware security key (such as a FIDO2 USB key) is phishing-resistant because
options: It performs cryptographic authentication bound to the site's origin and requires physical presence
It types the password for you
It stores passwords in the cloud
It works with any website password
explain: Unlike OTP codes, security keys cannot be tricked into authenticating a fake domain.

q: SIM swapping attacks target a victim by
options: Installing spyware via the app store
Convincing the carrier to move the victim's number to the attacker's SIM, hijacking SMS codes and calls
explain: Number port-out fraud defeats SMS-based MFA; carrier account PINs and app-based MFA mitigate it.

q: An evil twin attack is best defeated for corporate users by
options: Validating the RADIUS server's certificate on the client and using EAP-TLS/PEAP with strict checks
explain: If clients verify the authentication server's certificate, a fake AP cannot complete the handshake or harvest credentials.

q: Bluetooth 'bluejacking' is
options: Sending unsolicited messages to nearby Bluetooth devices (a nuisance), unlike bluesnarfing which steals data
Pairing without consent to play audio
explain: Bluejacking = unwanted messages; bluesnarfing = unauthorized data extraction; bluebugging = device control.

q: Faraday bags/cages are used in forensics and security to
options: Block all radio signals to/from a device, preventing remote wipe or tracking
explain: RF shielding isolates seized devices from cellular/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth until examination.

q: Privacy screens (polarizing filters) mitigate
options: Shoulder surfing/visual hacking by narrowing the display's viewing angle
explain: Privacy filters make off-angle viewing nearly impossible in public spaces.

q: Secure pull printing (badge/PIN release) prevents
options: Sensitive documents sitting unclaimed in the output tray
explain: Jobs are held until the owner authenticates at the device, protecting confidentiality.

q: Disabling AutoRun/AutoPlay for removable media reduces infections because
options: Malware on USB media cannot execute automatically when inserted
Files cannot be copied at all
explain: Autorun worms were a classic propagation path; disabling auto-execution breaks it.

q: Application allowlisting (such as Windows Defender Application Control) is stronger than blocklisting because
options: Only approved software can run; everything unknown is denied by default
explain: Deny-by-default flips the model: unknown malware has no path to execute even if never seen before.

q: Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules in Defender target behaviors such as
options: Office apps creating child processes or executables, and scripts obfuscating code
explain: ASR blocks the specific techniques malware abuses inside legitimate apps rather than signatures alone.

q: A TPM's Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs) are used in measured boot to
options: Store hashes of boot components so tampering with the boot chain is detectable
explain: Each boot stage extends PCRs with measurements; BitLocker can seal keys to expected PCR values.

q: Secure Boot's revocation database (dbx) exists to
options: Block known-bad or vulnerable bootloaders/signatures that were previously trusted
explain: When a signed bootloader is found vulnerable (e.g., BootHole), dbx revocation prevents it from loading.

q: Windows Hello for Business replaces passwords with
options: Asymmetric key pairs protected by TPM and unlocked by PIN/biometrics, authenticating to AD/Azure AD
explain: Hello for Business provisions device-bound keys, giving phishing-resistant SSO to domain resources.

q: LSA protection (RunAsPPL) helps prevent
options: Credential theft tools from reading LSASS process memory
explain: Running LSASS as a protected process blocks unprivileged code injection/memory reads used by credential dumpers.

q: Event ID 4625 in the Windows Security log records
options: A failed logon attempt (with the source and reason)
explain: 4625s are the raw material for detecting brute force and password spraying.

q: A worm differs from a virus in that a worm
options: Spreads between systems by itself over the network without needing a host file or user action
explain: Worms self-propagate (often via vulnerabilities); viruses attach to hosts/files and typically need user action.

q: A logic bomb is malware that
options: Executes its payload when a specific condition or date is met
explain: Logic bombs lie dormant until triggered—classically planted by insiders.

q: A Remote Access Trojan (RAT) gives an attacker
options: Ongoing remote control of the infected machine as if they were the user
explain: RATs provide persistent interactive access: screen, files, camera, and command execution.

q: Fileless malware is hard to detect because it
options: Lives in memory and abuses legitimate tools (PowerShell, WMI) instead of dropping files to disk
explain: 'Living off the land' with signed system tools evades file-based antivirus scanning.

q: Double-extortion ransomware groups increase pressure by
options: Stealing data first and threatening to publish it, in addition to encrypting it
explain: Even victims with good backups face the leak threat in double extortion.

q: A macro virus spreads primarily through
options: Malicious macros embedded in Office documents shared between users
explain: Macro malware rides documents; modern Office blocks internet-sourced macros by default.

q: A rootkit operating at kernel level is especially dangerous because it
options: Cannot be removed by rebooting only
Runs with the highest privileges and can hide processes, files, and itself from the OS and security tools
explain: Kernel rootkits subvert the very tools used to detect them; offline scans or rebuilds are the reliable cure.

q: Spyware and keyloggers share the trait that they
options: Covertly monitor user activity and exfiltrate the collected information
explain: Both are surveillance tools; stalkerware is the consumer-grade variant aimed at individuals.

q: Spear phishing differs from ordinary phishing in that it
options: Is targeted at a specific person/organization using researched personal details
explain: Research makes spear phishing far more convincing; whaling targets senior executives specifically.

q: Business Email Compromise (BEC) typically involves
options: Impersonating an executive or vendor to trick staff into wiring money or changing payment details
explain: BEC relies on authority and plausible context rather than malware—often from lookalike domains or compromised mailboxes.

q: A watering hole attack compromises
options: A legitimate website frequented by the target group, infecting its visitors
explain: Attackers poison a site the victims trust and wait for them to visit.

q: Typosquatting profits from
options: Registering misspelled versions of popular domains to catch mistyped visits (ads, phishing, malware)
explain: Users who fat-finger a URL land on the attacker's lookalike site.

q: Pharming redirects victims to fake sites by
options: Poisoning DNS resolution (or the hosts file) so a correct URL resolves to the attacker's server
explain: Unlike phishing links, pharming works even when the user types the right address.

q: Vishing is social engineering conducted via
explain: Vishing (voice phishing) includes help-desk impersonation and executive fraud calls; smishing is SMS.

q: The social engineering principle of 'authority' works because
options: People comply with requests that appear to come from someone in charge (executive, IT, law enforcement)
explain: Cialdini's principles—authority, urgency, scarcity, fear, likability, consensus—are the levers phishers pull.

q: Tailgating differs from piggybacking in that tailgating
options: Follows an authorized person through a secure door WITHOUT their knowledge/consent
Requires the employee to hold the door knowingly
explain: In piggybacking the insider knowingly lets the person in; in tailgating they are unaware—both defeat badge systems.

q: Dumpster diving is a security concern because
options: It is only a facilities issue
Discarded documents and media can reveal passwords, org charts, and sensitive data
explain: Shredding and media destruction policies exist because trash is an intelligence source.

q: Pretexting is best described as
options: Inventing a fabricated scenario (a pretext) to manipulate a victim into divulging information or access
explain: The pretext is the cover story that makes the request feel legitimate.

q: An Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) is characterized by
options: A well-resourced actor maintaining stealthy, long-term access to pursue specific objectives
explain: APTs (often nation-state) prioritize stealth and persistence over quick wins.

q: Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) used by defenders include
options: Known malicious file hashes, domains, and IP addresses from threat intelligence
explain: IOCs feed detection tools so known-bad artifacts are flagged across the environment.

q: Detonating a suspicious file in a sandbox means
options: Running it on the CEO's PC
Executing it in an isolated analysis environment to observe its behavior safely
explain: Sandboxes (including email-gateway attachment sandboxes) reveal behavior without risking production systems.

q: DMARC policies (p=quarantine or p=reject) instruct receiving servers to
options: Dispose of mail that fails SPF/DKIM alignment checks for the domain
Accept all mail from the domain
explain: DMARC turns SPF/DKIM results into enforceable handling, stopping direct domain spoofing when set to reject.

q: DKIM protects email by
options: Adding a cryptographic signature (with the sending domain's private key) that receivers verify via DNS
explain: DKIM proves the message was authorized by the domain and unaltered in transit (integrity, not confidentiality).

q: An 'External' warning banner on inbound email helps users by
options: Flagging messages that originated outside the organization so impersonation attempts stand out
explain: Display-name spoofing of executives is blunted when users see the external tag (combine with training—banners get ignored over time).

q: URL rewriting/defense in secure email gateways works by
options: Rewriting links so clicks are re-checked for safety at the moment of use (time-of-click protection)
explain: A URL safe at delivery may be weaponized later; time-of-click scanning catches that.

q: Display name spoofing succeeds when users
options: Use mobile email apps with small headers
Trust the friendly 'From' name without checking the actual email address/domain
explain: Attackers set the display name to the CEO's name while the address is an unrelated free-mail account.

q: A help-desk social engineering call (vishing IT) often aims to get the technician to
options: Reset a password or MFA enrollment without properly verifying the caller's identity
explain: MFA reset fraud (as in major 2023 breaches) bypasses strong auth at the process layer; strict callback/ID verification is the defense.

q: Security awareness training is most effective when it is
options: Ongoing, role-relevant, and paired with easy reporting (e.g., a phish report button) rather than blame
explain: Programs that reward reporting raise detection rates; shame-based programs drive incidents underground.

q: Shadow IT is a security risk primarily because
options: Unsanctioned apps and services hold company data outside security controls and visibility
explain: Unknown SaaS/file-sharing accounts bypass DLP, retention, and access reviews.

q: An insider threat differs from an external attacker in that the insider
options: Already has legitimate access, making misuse harder to distinguish from normal work
explain: Monitoring, least privilege, and separation of duties are the classic insider controls.

q: Separation of duties prevents fraud by ensuring
options: No single person can complete a sensitive process alone (e.g., create a vendor AND approve its payment)
explain: Splitting critical steps forces collusion, which is much harder and riskier for fraudsters.

q: Mandatory vacations and job rotation are security controls because they
options: Expose ongoing fraud or errors that require the perpetrator's constant presence to conceal
explain: Schemes that need daily tending unravel when someone else sits in the chair.

q: Access recertification (access reviews) requires managers to
options: Periodically re-approve each person's access so stale permissions are removed
explain: Reviews combat privilege creep as people change roles (the 'mover' problem).

q: The joiner-mover-leaver process matters because
options: Access must change promptly at each transition; leaver accounts disabled immediately at exit
explain: Most orphaned-account incidents trace to slow deprovisioning, especially for movers accumulating rights.

q: Data Loss Prevention (DLP) tools detect and block
options: Sensitive data (card numbers, SSNs, source code) leaving via email, web, USB, or print based on content inspection
explain: DLP classifies content and enforces policy on egress channels, with alerts or blocks.

q: A purple team exercise differs from separate red/blue exercises in that
options: Red (attack) and blue (defense) work together in real time, sharing findings so detection and response improve during the exercise itself
explain: Purple teaming turns findings into immediate defensive tuning instead of a report weeks later.

q: DNS filtering/sinkholing blocks malware by
options: Preventing resolution of known malicious domains so infected hosts cannot reach command-and-control
explain: If the C2 domain won't resolve, the malware is stranded; sinkholes also reveal infected machines by their queries.

q: A reverse proxy differs from a forward proxy in that it
options: Hides the client's identity from servers
Sits in front of servers, presenting them to clients (load balancing, WAF, TLS offload)
explain: Forward proxies serve clients; reverse proxies protect and publish servers.

q: A Web Application Firewall (WAF) protects against
options: DDoS only, at the network layer
Application-layer attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting against web apps
explain: WAFs inspect HTTP(S) semantics, filtering malicious requests that a network firewall would pass.

q: Signature-based detection's fundamental weakness is
options: It cannot recognize new or modified malware that has no known signature
explain: Zero-days and polymorphic variants evade signatures—hence behavioral/EDR layers.

q: Behavioral/heuristic analysis in modern endpoint protection watches for
options: Suspicious actions (mass file encryption, process injection, credential access) rather than known file hashes
explain: Behavioral engines catch novel malware by what it does—the basis of EDR/XDR.

q: EDR differs from traditional antivirus in that EDR
options: Continuously records endpoint activity for investigation and can isolate hosts and roll back changes
explain: EDR assumes breach: telemetry, hunting, containment, and remediation are its core value.

q: A SIEM's core job is to
options: Collect logs from across the environment, correlate events, and alert on patterns no single source would reveal
Back up the logs to tape
explain: Correlation turns scattered logs (a failed logon here, a VPN login there) into detectable incidents.

q: SOAR platforms extend a SOC by
options: Automating response playbooks (enrich, isolate, ticket) to speed analyst workflows
explain: Security Orchestration, Automation and Response reduces manual toil in triage and containment.

q: Threat intelligence feeds are most useful when they are
options: Actionable: mapped to the organization's environment and fed into detection/blocking tools
explain: Intel that never changes a control is trivia; the value is in automated enforcement and hunting hypotheses.

q: A responsible bug bounty program gives an organization
options: Legal immunity for attackers of any kind
Crowdsourced vulnerability discovery from vetted external researchers, paid per valid finding within a defined scope and rules of engagement
Free penetration tests with no scope limits
explain: Scope and safe-harbor rules are what separate bounty research from attacks.

q: An implicit deny at the end of a firewall ACL means
options: Any traffic not explicitly permitted is dropped
explain: Default-deny posture: rules permit known-good traffic; everything else hits the implicit deny.

q: Egress filtering controls
options: Outbound traffic, blocking exfiltration channels and unauthorized services leaving the network
explain: Restricting what can leave (ports, destinations) blunts C2 callbacks and data theft.

q: A stateful firewall improves on a stateless packet filter by
options: Tracking connection state and automatically allowing legitimate return traffic
explain: State tables let replies to permitted outbound sessions back in without extra rules.

q: A next-generation firewall (NGFW) adds over a traditional firewall
options: Application awareness, integrated IPS, and user-identity-based rules
explain: NGFWs identify apps regardless of port and fold in intrusion prevention and identity.

q: A Unified Threat Management (UTM) appliance is aimed at
options: Combining firewall, IPS, antivirus, content filtering, and more in one box for smaller organizations
explain: UTM trades depth for simplicity: one console, many security functions.

q: Microsegmentation improves internal security by
options: Enforcing firewall policies between individual workloads inside the network, not just at the perimeter
explain: East-west controls limit lateral movement after a breach of one internal system.

q: WPA3's SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) handshake improves over WPA2-PSK by
options: Resisting offline dictionary attacks against a captured handshake and providing forward secrecy
Removing the need for passwords entirely
explain: SAE (Dragonfly) means a captured exchange cannot be brute-forced offline; each session gets unique keys.

q: WPA2-Enterprise with 802.1X is preferred in companies because
options: Each user/device authenticates individually, so access can be revoked per person—unlike a shared PSK
explain: Per-user credentials kill the 'one shared Wi-Fi password for the whole office forever' problem.

q: A wireless intrusion prevention system (WIPS) can
options: Detect rogue APs and evil twins and actively deauthenticate clients connecting to them
explain: WIPS monitors the RF environment and can contain unauthorized wireless devices.

q: Bluetooth should be disabled on secure workstations when unused because
options: It expands the attack surface (pairing exploits, bluesnarfing) within physical proximity
explain: Short range is not no risk: proximity attacks and forgotten discoverable modes expose data.

q: RFID badges can be cloned with cheap readers; high-security facilities mitigate this with
options: Encrypted/smart credentials (e.g., SEOS/DESFire) plus MFA such as badge + PIN at critical doors
explain: Legacy 125 kHz prox cards are trivially copyable; modern encrypted credentials and a second factor close the hole.

q: An access control vestibule (mantrap) prevents
options: Tailgating: only one person is admitted at a time into the secured area
explain: Interlocking doors verify a single occupant (often with weight/biometric checks) before releasing the inner door.

q: Bollards in front of a building protect against
options: Vehicle ramming attacks against entrances and storefronts
explain: Bollards are rated physical barriers against vehicle-borne attacks.

q: Clean-agent fire suppression is used in server rooms because it
options: Extinguishes fire without water/chemical residue that would destroy electronics
explain: Gaseous agents (e.g., FM-200, Novec) suppress fire while leaving equipment intact—life safety rules still apply.

q: Faraday cages in a workplace context are used for
options: Shielding sensitive areas or test devices from RF signals (and emissions)
explain: RF shielding prevents wireless communication and reduces emanation leakage.

q: Air-gapped systems are protected by
options: Complete physical isolation from other networks, so data moves only via controlled media
explain: Air gaps (used for the most sensitive systems) trade convenience for near-total network isolation—media handling becomes the risk.

q: Immutable backups defend against ransomware by
options: Eliminating the need for off-site copies
Preventing backup data from being modified or deleted for a set retention period, even by admins/attackers
explain: Attackers target backups first; immutability (and the 3-2-1-1-0 rule's '1 immutable') guarantees a clean restore point.

q: The '0' in the 3-2-1-1-0 backup rule stands for
explain: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 off-site, 1 offline/immutable, 0 verification errors.

q: NIST SP 800-88 media sanitization levels are
options: Clear, Purge, and Destroy—increasing assurance methods for removing data from media
explain: Clear (logical), Purge (degauss/crypto-erase), Destroy (physical) map to media type and data sensitivity.

q: Degaussing works on magnetic media but is ineffective on SSDs because
options: SSDs store data as electrical charges in flash cells, not magnetic domains
SSDs have no platters to spin
explain: For flash, use crypto-erase (destroy keys) or physical destruction per 800-88.

q: A certificate of destruction provides
options: Encryption keys for the new drive
Documented proof that specific media was sanitized/destroyed (serial numbers, method, date, witness)
explain: Certificates complete the chain of custody for compliance audits.

q: Data classification labels (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted) drive
options: Handling rules: encryption, sharing limits, retention, and destruction per sensitivity
explain: Classification tells every control downstream how to treat the data.

q: Watermarking documents helps security by
options: Attributing leaks: visible or forensic marks identify whose copy was disclosed
