explain: Per-recipient watermarks deter leaks and support investigations when documents surface.

q: Rights management (IRM/DRM) on documents enforces
options: Persistent controls—no forwarding, expiry, view-only—even after the file leaves the network
explain: IRM travels with the file, extending policy beyond the perimeter (e.g., sensitivity labels with encryption).

q: A password manager improves user security mainly by
options: Storing passwords in the browser only
Enabling a unique, strong password for every account without memorization burden
explain: Unique passwords per site neutralize credential stuffing; the vault itself is protected by a strong master password + MFA.

q: Passphrase guidance favors
options: Long, memorable phrases (4+ random words) over short, complex strings
explain: Length dominates entropy for human-usable secrets; NIST guidance also drops forced periodic changes absent compromise.

q: Security keys and authenticator apps are preferred over SMS codes because
options: SMS is vulnerable to SIM swapping and number porting fraud
Phones cannot receive SMS in offices
explain: Out-of-band SMS rides the phone network's weak identity checks; TOTP/hardware keys stay on the device.

q: A honeypot's value in an enterprise is
options: Early warning: any interaction with a decoy system is suspicious by definition, generating high-fidelity alerts
explain: Decoys have no legitimate users, so touches are almost never false positives.

q: Threat hunting differs from alert-driven monitoring in that hunting
options: Waits for the SIEM to fire
Proactively searches for signs of compromise based on hypotheses, assuming attackers may already be inside
explain: Hunting is human-led, intel-driven searching for what signatures missed.

q: A vulnerability scan differs from a penetration test in that a scan
options: Is illegal without permission (scans are not)
Automatically enumerates known vulnerabilities; a pentest actively exploits weaknesses to prove impact
explain: Scans find potential issues at scale; pentests demonstrate real-world exploitability and chaining.

q: Risk is commonly expressed as
options: Likelihood × impact (threat × vulnerability, in qualitative models)
explain: Risk assessments weigh how likely an event is against how bad it would be to prioritize treatment.

q: The four standard risk treatments are
options: Mitigate, accept, transfer (e.g., insurance), and avoid
explain: Every identified risk gets a deliberate treatment decision, documented and owned.

q: A compensating control is
options: An alternative safeguard used when the primary control cannot be implemented (e.g., extra monitoring where patching is impossible)
explain: PCI DSS formalized the concept: equivalent protection when the letter of a requirement can't be met.

q: Defense in depth means
options: Layering independent controls so no single failure exposes the asset
explain: Perimeter + segmentation + endpoint + identity + backups each catch what others miss.

q: A password manager advertises a 'zero-knowledge' architecture, meaning
options: The provider can reset any vault entry for you
Passwords are stored in plaintext for speed
Vaults are encrypted/decrypted only on the user's device with keys derived from the master password—the provider cannot read the stored passwords
explain: Zero-knowledge is why a manager vendor's breach doesn't expose vault contents—and why a forgotten master password can mean a lost vault.

q: An allowlist approach to USB storage in high-security areas might use
options: Device control policies permitting only specific encrypted, company-issued drives by serial/ID
Blocking the USB ports physically with glue only
Allowing all drives but scanning monthly
explain: Endpoint device control can whitelist sanctioned encrypted media and block everything else.

q: SmartScreen and reputation services warn users when
options: A downloaded program or site has an unknown or malicious reputation
explain: Reputation checks are a last-moment guardrail against fresh malware and phishing sites.

q: Windows Defender Firewall profiles apply different rule sets for
options: Domain, Private, and Public network locations
explain: The firewall tightens automatically on Public networks and relaxes appropriately on trusted ones.

q: A host-based firewall adds value beyond the network firewall because it
options: Protects the machine on hostile networks and can control outbound connections per application
explain: Host firewalls travel with the laptop and enforce per-app egress rules.

q: MAC address randomization on phones protects privacy by
options: Using rotating fake MACs for Wi-Fi probing so the device cannot be tracked across locations
explain: Randomization defeats retail/analytics tracking based on probe requests; networks may still see a per-network MAC.

q: Disabling unused network services and ports on a workstation is an example of
explain: Every listening service is a door; hardening closes the unneeded ones.

q: Banner grabs and login page warnings ('Authorized use only') support security by
options: Providing legal notice that monitoring is in effect and unauthorized access is prohibited
explain: Warning banners strengthen prosecution and set user expectations of monitoring.

q: Security baselines from vendors (e.g., Microsoft security baselines, CIS Benchmarks) provide
options: Pre-tested, recommended configuration standards to harden systems consistently
explain: Baselines encode expert consensus so each machine doesn't get hand-tuned security.

q: Group Policy 'Password must meet complexity requirements' enforces
options: Passwords mixing character classes and not containing the account name
explain: Complexity works with length policies; modern guidance emphasizes length and breach-password screening.

q: A rainbow table attack uses
options: Precomputed chains of password hashes to reverse common passwords quickly (defeated by salting)
explain: Rainbow tables trade storage for speed; unique salts make precomputation useless per-account.

q: A dictionary attack differs from brute force in that it
options: Tries likely words/phrases (and mutations) instead of every possible combination
explain: Dictionaries exploit human password choices; brute force guarantees eventual success given time.

q: Pass-the-hash attacks work because
options: Hashes can be decrypted with the username
Windows stores passwords in plain text
The hash is the same as the username
The attacker uses a stolen NTLM hash to authenticate without knowing the plaintext password
explain: NTLM authentication accepts the hash itself as proof—hence Credential Guard/LAPS and disabling NTLM where possible.

q: MFA fatigue (push bombing) is countered most directly by
options: Number matching: the user must enter digits shown on the sign-in screen into the authenticator prompt
explain: Number matching proves the user is actually at the sign-in attempt, defeating blind approval spam.

q: SQL injection is prevented at the application level primarily by
options: Parameterized queries/prepared statements that keep user input separate from SQL code
explain: Input validation helps, but parameterization is the structural fix; WAFs are a compensating layer.

q: Cross-site scripting (XSS) lets an attacker
options: Run malicious scripts in victims' browsers in the context of a vulnerable site
Steal the server's private key directly
explain: Stored/reflected XSS abuses a site's trust in user input; output encoding and CSP are the defenses.

q: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) tricks a browser into
options: Submitting an unwanted request to a site where the user is already authenticated
explain: The site sees a valid session cookie; anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies are the standard mitigations.

q: Directory (path) traversal attacks use sequences like ../ to
options: List the site's directory for SEO
Escape the web root and access files elsewhere on the server
explain: Improper input sanitization lets attackers reach configuration files and credentials outside the intended folder.

q: Privilege escalation vulnerabilities allow an attacker to
options: Reset any user's password by email
Move from a low-privilege account to admin/SYSTEM/root control
explain: Escalation (vertical) is distinct from lateral movement (horizontal, same privilege, more machines).

q: A zero-day vulnerability is one that
options: Is exploited before the vendor has released a patch (the vendor has had zero days to fix it)
explain: Zero-days justify defense-in-depth and virtual patching (IPS/WAF rules) while the vendor works.

q: Software supply-chain attacks compromise targets by
options: Inserting malicious code into a legitimate vendor's software or update that customers trust and install
explain: SolarWinds-style attacks turn the update channel into the delivery mechanism—hence code signing and verification.

q: Session hijacking via cookie theft is mitigated by
options: HttpOnly and Secure cookie flags, TLS everywhere, and short session lifetimes with re-authentication for sensitive actions
explain: If malware or XSS steals a session cookie, flags and lifetimes limit its usefulness.

q: An IMSI catcher (cell-site simulator, 'stingray') attacks mobile users by
options: Pretending to be a cell tower so phones connect to it, enabling interception and location tracking
explain: Forcing connections (often with downgrades to weaker protocols) is the core technique; modern 4G/5G mutual authentication raises the bar.

q: Juice jacking is the risk that
options: A public USB charging port/cable is modified to steal data or install malware; a USB data blocker prevents it
explain: Charge-only adapters ('USB condoms') pass power but no data lines, neutralizing the attack.

q: Quishing is phishing delivered via
options: QR codes that lead to credential-harvesting sites, often bypassing email link scanning
explain: QR codes hide the URL from both users and some filters; users should preview the destination before opening.

q: Split-tunnel VPN configurations carry the security trade-off that
options: The VPN is twice as fast to connect
No encryption is used at all
Only work traffic goes through the tunnel; the user's other internet traffic bypasses corporate inspection and controls
explain: Split tunneling saves bandwidth but leaves a bridge between the internet and the corporate network on the same machine.

q: The most important hardening step for a home-office router is
options: Change the default admin password, update firmware, and use WPA2-AES/WPA3 with a strong passphrase (disable WPS and remote admin)
Set the transmit power to maximum
Rename the network to the company name
explain: Default credentials and unpatched firmware are the top home-router compromises; WPS PIN mode is notoriously weak.

q: On public Wi-Fi, the safest practice for sensitive work is
options: Avoid it or use a trusted VPN and verify the exact network name with staff; prefer cellular when possible
Connect to the strongest open signal
explain: Open networks allow sniffing and evil twins; a VPN encrypts traffic beyond the local segment.

q: Modern mobile OS runtime permissions improve security by
options: Granting all permissions at install permanently
Asking users to grant sensitive permissions (location, camera, contacts) per app at first use, revocable anytime
explain: Per-app, revocable permissions replaced the old all-or-nothing install-time model.

q: Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) apps add
options: On-device detection of malicious apps, risky networks, and OS tampering beyond basic MDM controls
explain: MTD is the mobile analog of endpoint protection, feeding risk signals into conditional access.

q: Always-on VPN on a managed phone ensures
options: All traffic is tunneled through the corporate VPN before reaching the internet, with connections blocked if the tunnel drops
explain: Always-on (with lockdown/kill-switch behavior) prevents leaks when the tunnel fails.

q: Android's Private DNS feature (DNS over TLS) protects mobile users by
options: Encrypting DNS queries to a chosen resolver so local networks cannot snoop or tamper with them
explain: Encrypted DNS (DoT/DoH) closes the plain-text DNS snooping hole on untrusted networks.

q: A laptop cable lock is a deterrent against
options: Opportunistic physical theft (snatch-and-grab) in public/shared spaces
explain: Cable locks use the Kensington slot; they delay, not defeat, a determined thief—but stop walk-aways.

q: Cross-cut (micro-cut) shredders are preferred over strip-cut for sensitive documents because
options: They reduce paper to much smaller particles that are impractical to reconstruct
explain: Higher DIN security levels (P-4 and up) specify particle sizes for confidential material.

q: A clean desk policy requires
options: Desks to be cleaned daily by staff
Sensitive documents and media to be locked away when unattended, with screens locked
explain: Clean desk + clear screen reduce opportunistic information theft in offices and home workspaces.

q: Visitor management best practice in secure facilities includes
options: Signing in, identity verification, visible badges, and escorting visitors at all times in sensitive areas
Letting visitors roam if they look professional
explain: Escorts and logs close the social-engineering door that open offices create.

q: Passive infrared (PIR) sensors detect intruders by sensing
options: Changes in infrared heat signatures (body heat moving across zones)
explain: PIR is the standard motion detector in alarm systems and automatic lighting.

q: Reviewing door access logs after an incident helps investigators
options: Reconstruct who badged into which areas and when, correlating with camera footage
explain: Badge logs are often the timeline backbone of physical incident investigations.

q: Tamper Protection in Windows Security prevents
options: Malware (or rogue scripts) from disabling Defender settings such as real-time protection
explain: With Tamper Protection on, Defender's security settings can only be changed through proper channels.

q: Cloud-delivered protection in Microsoft Defender Antivirus provides
options: Near-instant protection against newly discovered malware via cloud lookups, complementing local signatures
explain: Cloud protection shortens the gap between a new threat's discovery and client protection.

q: Network protection (a Defender feature) blocks
options: Connections to malicious/phishing domains and low-reputation sites at the network level
explain: It extends SmartScreen-style reputation checks beyond the browser to other apps and processes.

q: PUA protection in Windows guards against
options: Potentially unwanted applications—adware, bundleware, and cryptominers that are not strictly malware
explain: PUAs degrade performance and privacy without crossing the malware line; blocking them is a policy choice.

q: Data Execution Prevention (DEP) and ASLR are exploit mitigations that
options: Prevent code execution from data pages and randomize memory layout to make exploitation unreliable
explain: These OS features raise the cost of memory-corruption exploits—ASLR randomizes addresses, DEP marks data non-executable.

q: Network Level Authentication (NLA) for Remote Desktop improves security by
options: Authenticating the user before a full remote session is created, reducing the server's exposed attack surface
explain: NLA (CredSSP) means unauthenticated users never reach the logon screen, cutting resource abuse and exploit exposure.

q: Exposing RDP directly to the internet is dangerous mainly because
options: It is constantly brute-forced and targeted by exploits; it belongs behind a VPN or RD Gateway with MFA
explain: Bots scan for 3389 around the clock; gateway + MFA is the standard exposure pattern.

q: Hardening SSH on a Linux server includes
options: Key-only authentication, disabling direct root login, and limiting users; optionally rate-limiting with fail2ban
Allowing password auth from anywhere forever
explain: SSH keys plus no root password login closes the brute-force door that password auth leaves open.

q: fail2ban protects Linux services by
options: Monitoring logs for repeated authentication failures and temporarily banning offending IPs via the firewall
explain: It turns brute-force noise into automatic, time-boxed firewall bans.

q: macOS System Integrity Protection (SIP) prevents
options: Even root from modifying critical system files and processes, limiting rootkit persistence
explain: SIP keeps core macOS untouchable, forcing attackers (and admins) to work around it rather than through it.

q: XProtect is macOS's built-in
options: Signature-based malware detection/remediation that updates silently in the background
explain: XProtect (plus Gatekeeper and MRT) is Apple's layered anti-malware answer—no separate AV required for baseline protection.

q: Browser extensions are a security risk that should be managed by
options: Allowing only vetted extensions from official stores and reviewing requested permissions
Giving extensions all permissions they ask for
explain: Extensions run with broad page access; rogue or sold-off extensions are a real data-theft channel.

q: Enabling Secure DNS (DNS over HTTPS) in a browser
options: Makes all websites load over HTTPS
Encrypts DNS lookups between the browser and resolver, hiding them from the local network
explain: DoH protects name-resolution privacy in the browser, though enterprises may manage it via policy.

q: Restricting the local Administrators group via Group Policy (Restricted Groups / local group policy) defends against
options: Users and malware running with standing local admin rights (and lateral movement using them)
explain: Removing everyday users from local admin is one of the highest-value hardening steps.

q: Creating a Windows Firewall rule to allow an app should be scoped by
options: Allowing all profiles and all addresses by default
Limiting the rule to the needed profile and, where possible, specific remote IPs/subnets and ports
explain: Least-privilege firewall rules reduce exposure compared to broad allow-any rules.

q: Change and configuration baselines protect security because
options: Deviations from a known-good hardened configuration become visible and investigable
explain: Baseline drift detection is how configuration attacks and mistakes are caught.

q: The purpose of a DMZ 'jump box' (jump server) for administration is
options: To force all admin access to internal systems through one hardened, logged chokepoint
explain: Jump hosts centralize privileged access for monitoring and control.

q: A Windows PC has become slow to boot over months. The most effective first diagnostic is
options: Task Manager's Startup tab and a clean-boot comparison to find heavy auto-start items
explain: Boot slowdowns accumulate from auto-start apps and services; Startup impact ratings and clean boot isolate them.

q: A user's Windows PIN suddenly shows 'This option is currently unavailable.' A common repair is
options: Delete the Ngc folder contents (in Safe Mode/admin context) and set up the PIN again
explain: Corrupted NGC container data breaks Hello credentials; clearing it lets Windows rebuild the PIN store.

q: A fingerprint reader vanishes from sign-in options after an update. Beyond the driver, check
options: The Windows Biometric Service is running
explain: Hello biometrics depend on the Windows Biometric Service; a stopped service removes the option.

q: Sound is fine in most apps but one game is silent. The likely setting is
options: Per-app volume/output in the Volume Mixer (or the app's exclusive-mode setting)
explain: Windows remembers per-app levels and output devices; check App volume and device preferences first.

q: A Bluetooth headset pairs successfully but never connects for audio. The standard fix sequence is
options: Replace the headset battery with a larger one
Remove the device, re-pair it, and confirm the Bluetooth Support Service is running
explain: Stale pairings corrupt the connection profile; removing and re-pairing rebuilds it.

q: Wi-Fi disconnects every time a laptop sleeps or the lid closes, taking a minute to return. A quick fix is
options: In Device Manager, uncheck 'Allow the computer to turn off this device to save power' for the wireless adapter
explain: Aggressive adapter power management drops the radio during sleep transitions.

q: A network printer shows 'Offline' in Windows although it is powered and pingable. A classic fix is
options: In the printer's port settings, uncheck 'SNMP Status Enabled' (or set the correct community)
Replace the printer's network cable with a longer one
explain: Bogus SNMP replies make Windows mark the queue offline; disabling SNMP status monitoring cures it.

q: Users suddenly get error 0x0000011b when connecting to a shared printer after a Windows security update. The cause is
options: The printer is out of paper
Hardened RPC/point-and-print authentication changes; patch the print server fully or apply the documented registry mitigation
explain: PrintNightmare-era patches changed spooler RPC authentication, breaking older print servers until fully patched/configured.

q: The default printer keeps changing to the last-used printer. The setting to disable is
explain: That convenience feature sets the default to whichever printer was used most recently.

q: Shared printer connections keep prompting some users for credentials after policy hardening. The likely area is
options: Guest/insecure logon restrictions (SMB signing/guest auth blocks) between client and print host
explain: Modern Windows blocks insecure guest authentication to shares/printers by default; proper accounts are the fix.

q: After connecting a second monitor, windows open on a screen that is no longer attached. To recover a lost window, use
options: Select the app on the taskbar, then press Alt+Space and Move (or Win+arrow keys) to bring it back
explain: Off-screen windows retain coordinates; the system menu Move with arrow keys drags them onto a live display.

q: A laptop's compact keyboard types numbers when pressing letter keys on the right side. The cause is
options: Num Lock is on, activating the embedded numeric keypad layer (use Fn+NumLock to toggle)
explain: Many laptops overlay a numpad on letter keys; NumLock state is the usual culprit.

q: A gamer keeps opening the Sticky Keys prompt mid-game when tapping Shift. The fix is
options: Turn off the 'press Shift five times' shortcut in Accessibility keyboard settings
explain: The accessibility shortcut itself can be disabled without turning the feature off entirely.

q: Desktop icons all disappeared but files are still in the Desktop folder. The likely cause is
options: The files were deleted by Windows Update
'Show desktop icons' was toggled off (right-click desktop > View), or tablet/rotation state changed
explain: Icon visibility is a view setting; the files usually remain untouched.

q: The taskbar search box does nothing when typing. A quick service-level check is
options: Restart the Windows Search service and the CTF Loader (ctfmon) for text input
explain: Taskbar search depends on Search indexing services and ctfmon for input; restarting both revives it.

q: A dual-boot Windows/Linux user finds Windows time is wrong by several hours after using Linux. The fix is
options: Replace the CMOS battery every month
Set the time zone to UTC in Windows
Tell Linux to use local time (or set Windows' RealTimeIsUniversal) because Linux defaults the hardware clock to UTC
explain: Linux keeps the RTC in UTC; Windows expects local time—aligning one side ends the tug-of-war.

q: Windows Spotlight is stuck on the same lock-screen image for weeks. A common reset is
options: Re-register/reset the Spotlight content settings (clear its cache under the ContentDeliveryManager package)
explain: Corrupt Spotlight cache/assets freeze rotation; resetting the package data restarts fresh downloads.

q: The News and Interests/widgets panel is using notable CPU and memory on a work PC. The clean fix is
options: Turn off Widgets from taskbar settings (or policy on managed machines)
explain: Widgets run web content continuously; disabling the feature removes the overhead.

q: A laptop offers no Sleep option in the power menu after a driver change. Restoring it usually involves
options: Restoring power plan defaults and ensuring the graphics/chipset drivers support modern standby states
explain: Missing sleep states are usually driver/plan issues; 'powercfg /a' shows which states the platform supports.

q: Hibernate is missing from the shutdown options. It can be re-enabled with
options: powercfg /hibernate on, then checking it in 'Choose what the power buttons do'
explain: The hiberfil.sys and the menu checkbox both depend on hibernation being enabled.

q: Airplane mode appears stuck ON and the toggle is greyed out. After a reboot, the next checks are
options: Device Manager (re-enable the radio/collection device) and the Radio Management Service
explain: A disabled 'airplane mode collection' device or a stuck service leaves radios off with a greyed toggle.

q: A Windows Hello face sign-in fails with 'camera not found' though the webcam works in apps. The likely conflict is
options: Another app or the antivirus is blocking the Hello IR camera, or the biometric service needs restarting
explain: Hello uses the IR camera through a protected path; security software and service faults are common causes.

q: After a feature update, several users report the Start menu won't open. A standard repair is
options: Re-register the Shell Experience/Start menu packages for the affected profiles via PowerShell
explain: Corrupted shell package registrations break Start; re-registering the AppX shell components fixes it.

q: File Explorer keeps crashing and restarting when opening a folder with videos. A probable cause is
options: The folder has too many files, always
A faulty thumbnail handler/shell extension (or a corrupt thumbnail cache)
explain: Shell extensions hook Explorer; disabling third-party handlers and clearing the thumbnail cache isolates it.

q: A specific website renders blank in Edge/Chrome but works in another browser. The first steps are
options: Clear that site's cookies/cache and test in an InPrivate/Incognito window (extensions off)
explain: Incognito isolates extensions and cached data—the two most common single-browser causes.

q: Clicking links in emails opens the wrong browser even after defaults were set. Check
options: The HTTP/HTTPS and .htm/.html associations specifically (protocol handlers can differ from the 'default browser' summary)
explain: Windows tracks per-protocol associations; a stale HTTPS handler keeps stealing links.

q: An app opens but its window is completely off-screen after undocking. Besides keyboard move tricks, Windows offers
options: Cascade windows or the display-settings 'make this my main display' reset to force re-layout
explain: Undocking coordinate bugs strand windows; taskbar Cascade forces all windows onto visible displays.

q: Screen orientation flipped upside down after a cat walked on the keyboard. The quick restore is
options: Ctrl+Alt+Up Arrow (on supported Intel graphics) or Settings > Display > Orientation = Landscape
explain: Graphics hotkeys rotate the display; locking rotation in settings prevents repeats.

q: Touchpad gestures (two-finger scroll, three-finger swipe) stopped after an update. The fix path is
options: Reinstall the precision touchpad driver and check Settings > Bluetooth & devices > Touchpad gestures are enabled
explain: Gesture support lives in the touchpad driver/settings; updates occasionally reset both.

q: Mouse pointer moves on its own in small drifts on a laptop. A frequent cause is
options: A failing/dirty touchpad registering phantom input—disable the touchpad when a mouse is connected to test
explain: Phantom touchpad input is a classic drift cause; isolating it confirms hardware vs. software.

q: Windows reports 'No audio output device is installed' after an update, though hardware is fine in BIOS. The fix is
options: Reinstall the audio driver and confirm the Windows Audio service is running (check for the update's generic driver)
explain: Updates sometimes swap in a broken/generic audio driver; the vendor driver plus service check restores sound.

q: One user cannot print to any printer; others on the same PC can. Test first whether
options: Their profile's print settings or credentials are the issue: sign in as another user to isolate profile vs. machine
explain: Profile-scoped faults follow the user; machine faults affect every account on the box.

q: A mapped network drive shows a red X at logon but works when clicked. This is usually
options: A timing artifact: Explorer maps the drive before the network is fully ready; it reconnects on access
explain: Red-X-at-logon is a long-standing cosmetic reconnect timing issue, not data loss.

q: Windows time keeps drifting on a domain PC even after manual correction. Investigate
options: The time service (w32time) source and the domain hierarchy; the PDC emulator is the authority
explain: Domain members must sync from the DC/PDC chain; a broken w32time config breaks Kerberos and logs too.

q: A PC wakes instantly every time it is put to sleep. Use this command to find the culprit:
explain: powercfg reports the last wake source—usually a NIC, USB device, or scheduled timer.

q: Clipboard history (Win+V) does not work for one user. Enable/fix via
options: Settings > System > Clipboard: turn on Clipboard history (and check policy on managed devices)
explain: Clipboard history is off by default in some builds and controllable by policy.

q: The Snipping Tool shortcut (Win+Shift+S) stopped working. Common fixes are
options: Repair/Reset the Snipping Tool app in Settings and verify the Print Screen key setting in Accessibility
explain: App corruption and the PrtScn-to-snip toggle are the frequent causes.

q: A user's Recycle Bin constantly reports corruption on one drive. The repair is
options: Delete the hidden $Recycle.Bin folder for that drive from an elevated prompt so Windows recreates it
explain: A damaged per-drive recycle store produces endless prompts; recreating it is the documented fix.

q: Thumbnails no longer preview photos in Explorer. Check
options: Folder Options/Performance settings: 'Always show icons, never thumbnails' is off, and clear the thumbnail cache
explain: A single checkbox (or a full thumbnail cache) kills previews while files remain fine.

q: Opening any folder spawns a brand-new Explorer window. The setting is
options: Folder Options > 'Open each folder in the same window' (General tab)
explain: An Explorer browsing option toggled by some tweakers causes the new-window behavior.

q: A Microsoft Store app crashes instantly on launch after an update. The built-in repair sequence is
options: Settings > Apps > the app > Advanced options: try Repair first, then Reset if needed
explain: Repair keeps data; Reset wipes the app's local state—the escalation path for Store apps.

q: An MSI installation fails with error 1603. The technician's best next step is
options: Run the install with verbose logging (/L*v) or check the MSI log in %temp% to find the failing action
explain: 1603 is a generic fatal error; the verbose log names the custom action or prerequisite that actually failed.

q: A user sees 'This app can't run on your PC' for a freshly downloaded program. The most common causes are
options: Architecture mismatch (32-bit vs 64-bit/ARM) or the PC being in S mode
The PC needs a new IP address
explain: Check the download matches the CPU architecture and that S mode isn't blocking non-Store software.

q: An application works when run as administrator but fails for the standard user. The real problem is usually
options: The app writes to protected locations (Program Files/registry HKLM); fix permissions or update the app—don't just run as admin forever
The user needs a new PC
explain: Legacy apps assuming admin rights break under standard accounts; shims or vendor updates are the durable fix.

q: Outlook reports it cannot open the OST and suggests deleting it. Deleting an OST is safe because
options: OSTs contain the only copy of email
It is a local cached copy; Outlook rebuilds it from the Exchange/365 server
explain: OST = offline cache (unlike PST archives); a corrupt OST is deleted and resynchronized. Unsent drafts in outbox are the exception to check.

q: Outlook search suddenly returns no results for recent mail. The fix path is
options: Check Outlook's indexing status and rebuild the search index (File > Options > Search > Indexing Options)
explain: Outlook search rides the Windows Search index; a stuck/corrupt index is rebuilt, not the mailbox.

q: Outlook is stuck showing 'Disconnected' though the network is fine. A sneaky cause is
options: Work Offline mode was toggled on (Send/Receive tab)
The user has too many folders, always
explain: Work Offline survives restarts and mimics a server outage.

q: Word and Excel start very slowly and sometimes hang. A leading suspect is
options: A faulty third-party COM add-in; test by starting the app in its Safe Mode (winword /safe)
explain: Office safe mode disables add-ins; re-enable them one at a time to find the offender.

q: PowerPoint presentations show substituted fonts on a colleague's PC. To prevent this, the author should
options: Embed fonts in the file (File > Options > Save > Embed fonts) or use standard fonts
explain: Font embedding (where licenses allow) travels the typefaces with the presentation.

q: A legacy Office file's Normal.dotm template is corrupt, causing Word crashes on launch. The fix is
options: Rename/delete Normal.dotm; Word recreates a clean one at next start
explain: A damaged global template breaks every launch; regeneration is safe (custom styles/macros in it are the caveat).

q: The default search engine in a user's browser changed itself and results are full of ads. After removing the culprit extension, also
options: Reset the browser's search engine/shortcut settings and scan for malware; check browser shortcut targets for appended URLs
explain: Hijackers persist via extensions, settings, and even modified shortcuts; all three need checking.

q: Every HTTPS site shows 'Your connection is not private' on one PC only, starting today. First check
options: The system date/time (a wrong clock invalidates certificates)
explain: Certificate validity windows depend on the clock; a reset clock breaks every secure site at once.

q: After malware cleanup, browsers cannot load any pages but ping works. A leftover setting to check is
options: A bogus proxy configured in Internet Settings (and reset WinHTTP proxy with netsh winhttp reset proxy)
explain: Malware often points browsers at a dead proxy; the setting survives the malware's removal.

q: Chrome reports every download as 'Virus scan failed' after an antivirus change. The cause is usually
options: The registered antivirus attachment-scan integration is broken; repair/reinstall the AV or adjust Chrome's scan settings
explain: Chrome delegates scanning; a broken AV registration makes every scan 'fail'.

q: wsreset.exe is the standard fix when
options: The Microsoft Store or its apps are stuck downloading/updating (it clears the Store cache)
explain: wsreset clears the Store cache without removing apps and reopens the Store.

q: OneDrive shows red X sync errors on many files in a deep folder tree. A common hidden cause is
options: The full file path exceeds Windows' path length limits, or filenames contain invalid characters
The user has too many monitors
explain: Long paths (legacy 260-char) and characters like < > : " | ? * break sync; renaming/shortening fixes it.

q: OneDrive is stuck on 'Processing changes' for days. The documented reset is
options: Close OneDrive and run %localappdata%\Microsoft\OneDrive\onedrive.exe /reset, then relaunch it
explain: The /reset switch rebuilds the sync database state without deleting files.

q: A user wants files from SharePoint/OneDrive to free local space but stay visible in Explorer. Set them to
options: 'Free up space' (online-only) after confirming they are fully synced
explain: Online-only placeholders keep the namespace visible while reclaiming disk.

q: Teams/Zoom callers say the user's microphone sounds robotic and cuts out. A frequent Windows setting culprit is
options: Audio 'enhancements' (or exclusive-mode/sample-rate mismatch) in the sound device properties
explain: Vendor enhancements and sample-rate fights garble VoIP audio; disabling them is a standard fix.

q: A webcam shows 'Camera in use by another application' in Teams. The resolution is
options: Find and close the other app holding the camera (browser tab, camera app, another meeting tool) and check privacy permissions
explain: Only one app can own most cameras at a time; privacy settings can also block access per app.

q: Screen sharing shows a black window when sharing a streaming app (Netflix etc.). This is
options: A sign to reinstall the browser
Expected DRM/HDCP behavior: protected video renders black to capture tools
explain: Content protection blanks protected playback in captures; share a different window or use the service's own watch-party features.

q: Remote Desktop connects, then the session freezes within a minute. A client-side fix that often works is
options: Buy more RAM for the server first
Disable UDP transport for RDP (client setting/policy) or update the network driver; MTU issues on VPNs are another suspect
Open port 3389 to the whole internet as a test (and leave it)
explain: UDP-based RDP transport interacts badly with some NAT/VPN paths; forcing TCP is a known workaround.

q: A VPN client fails with error 809 when connecting to the office. This typically means
options: The VPN server is behind NAT and UDP 500/4500 traffic or the NAT-T registry setting needs attention; or the firewall blocks IPsec
The VPN client needs a new wallpaper
explain: Error 809 = the connection was prevented because the server didn't respond; NAT-T and firewall rules are the usual fixes.

q: An Excel workbook suddenly recalculates nothing: formulas show stale values until cells are edited. The setting is
options: Calculation Options switched to Manual (Formulas tab); set to Automatic
explain: Manual calculation (sometimes set by another workbook) leaves results stale.

q: A PDF prints garbled characters from one machine but fine from another. A reliable workaround is
options: Print the PDF 'as image' from the reader, and update/reinstall that machine's print driver
explain: Print-as-image rasterizes the page, bypassing font/driver rendering faults.

q: Windows Fax and Scan or a legacy Java app is blocked after updates. The pragmatic help-desk reality is
options: Install the oldest Java version from a random site
Legacy components are deprecated; migrate the workflow (modern scan apps, supported runtimes) rather than weakening security to revive them
explain: Keeping dead platforms alive creates bigger risks than migrating the workflow.

q: Installing a desktop app fails with 'Windows Installer service could not be accessed.' The checks are
options: Confirm the Windows Installer service isn't disabled, and re-register msiexec if needed
explain: A disabled/corrupted Installer service breaks all MSI installs; /regserver reregisters it.

q: An app worked yesterday; today it crashes on launch for ALL users after a Windows update. The best-documented path is
options: Check the update's known issues, and roll back the update or the app's recent patch; use Reliability Monitor to confirm the timeline
explain: Correlating the crash start with the update in Reliability Monitor points to the culprit change.

q: A database program (QuickBooks-style multi-user) throws network errors only in multi-user mode. The pattern points to
options: The hosting/firewall configuration on the file server (database service ports blocked)
explain: Multi-user accounting apps rely on a database service and specific ports on the host; single-user mode bypasses them.

q: Browser pages load but embedded videos never play after a driver update. A likely cause is
options: Hardware acceleration conflict with the new GPU driver; toggle the browser's hardware acceleration to test
explain: A broken GPU driver path breaks video decode/rendering in browsers; software rendering isolates it.

q: A user installed a second antivirus 'for extra safety' and the PC became extremely slow with random freezes. The problem is
options: Two real-time AV engines conflict (double scanning, driver contention); keep exactly one real-time AV
The hard drive is too small
explain: Competing AVs hook the same operations; Defender automatically steps aside for a registered third-party AV—two third-parties fight.

q: Outlook rules stopped running after a mailbox migration. The typical fix is
options: Recreate or re-enable the rules; rules tied to the old profile/store often don't survive migration
explain: Client-side rules reference folders/stores that changed; rebuilding them restores automation.

q: A user's calendar shows meetings an hour off after traveling. The fix is
options: Set the correct time zone in Windows AND the calendar app's own time zone setting (they can differ)
explain: Outlook/OWA have independent time zone settings; mismatches shift displayed times while the data stays correct.

q: Shared OneDrive folder a user relied on 'disappeared' from Explorer, replaced by an internet shortcut. This is
options: The result of the folder's sharing being changed/the owner moving it; the .url shortcut links to the web location—re-add the shared folder if still shared
A Windows bug with no cause
explain: When sync of a shared folder stops (permission/move changes), Explorer leaves a web shortcut in its place.

q: Google Drive/Dropbox created 'conflicted copy' files for a document edited on two machines. This happens when
options: The same file was modified on both devices before either could sync, so both versions were preserved
The cloud deleted the original maliciously
explain: Sync engines preserve both edits as conflicted copies rather than silently overwriting one.

q: Windows Search finds files but Outlook items remain unsearchable. Beyond the index, Outlook-specific check:
options: Ensure the Outlook profile's data files are included in indexing scope and the profile isn't damaged; test in a new Outlook profile
explain: Scoping and profile health gate Outlook indexing independently of file search.

q: An application logs 'Access denied' writing to its own folder under Program Files. The modern fix is
options: Give Everyone Full Control on Program Files
Redirect the app to write data to ProgramData or the user profile (per current Windows design); grant targeted permissions only if the vendor requires it
explain: Apps should never write into Program Files; data belongs in ProgramData/AppData. Loosening the whole tree is a security regression.

q: A legacy app shows tiny, blurry text on a 4K display while other apps look fine. The per-app fix is
options: Compatibility tab > Change high DPI settings > Override with 'System (Enhanced)' scaling
explain: DPI-unaware apps can be scaled by the system instead of bitmap-stretching themselves.

q: Store apps for a single user are broken (won't open, missing from Start) but work for other users. The likely fault is
options: That user's AppX registration/profile state; re-register apps for the user or rebuild the profile
explain: Per-user package registration corruption is profile-scoped—Repairs: re-register packages, then profile rebuild if needed.

q: A scheduled backup application runs interactively but its scheduled jobs silently fail. A common cause is
options: The task runs under an account lacking 'Log on as a batch job' rights or the stored password changed
The backup files are too large
explain: Batch logon rights and stale stored credentials are classic silent-failure causes for scheduled jobs.

q: A Linux user gets a graphical login loop: correct password returns them to the login screen. Common causes are
options: A full home/root filesystem or broken permissions on ~/.Xauthority (or a crashed session); check disk space and logs from a TTY
The kernel is too new always
explain: Login loops classically trace to no writable home (disk full) or session startup errors; Ctrl+Alt+F3 to a TTY reveals it.

q: After a package install on Debian/Ubuntu, apt reports broken dependencies. The standard repair is
options: sudo apt --fix-broken install (then apt update && apt upgrade)
explain: --fix-broken resolves half-configured packages and missing dependencies.

q: A Linux server's disk filled overnight because of logs. The journal-specific cleanup is
options: journalctl --vacuum-time/--vacuum-size to trim the systemd journal (and review logrotate)
explain: The journal can grow unboundedly; vacuum commands enforce retention limits.

q: On Linux, a newly copied script fails with 'Permission denied' when executed directly. The fix is
options: chmod +x the script (and ensure the filesystem isn't mounted noexec)
Run it as a different user
explain: Files land without the execute bit; chmod +x is the standard remedy.

q: SSH to a Linux host suddenly warns 'REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED.' After verifying the server wasn't compromised, the fix is
options: Remove the stale key with ssh-keygen -R <host> and re-accept the new one
Disable host key checking permanently for all hosts
explain: Rebuilt/re-IP'd servers present new host keys; clear the old known_hosts entry after out-of-band verification.

q: A Linux workstation boots to an initramfs/busybox prompt. This usually indicates
options: The root filesystem couldn't be mounted (often fixed by running fsck on it from the prompt or live media)
explain: Dropping to initramfs means early boot failed—frequently filesystem corruption needing fsck.

q: Wi-Fi disappears on a Linux laptop after a kernel update. A likely cause is
options: The router changed its password by itself
The out-of-tree Wi-Fi driver module (DKMS) failed to rebuild for the new kernel
explain: DKMS rebuild failures after kernel upgrades are the classic cause; reinstall headers/driver or boot the old kernel.

q: A Mac app downloaded from a vendor shows 'is damaged and can't be opened.' For a legitimately trusted app, the cause is usually
options: The Mac has a virus for sure
Gatekeeper quarantine on a broken/unsigned bundle; re-download, or remove the quarantine attribute (xattr) after verifying the source
The app needs a new Mac
explain: Damaged/disk-image errors commonly trace to quarantine flags or corrupt downloads, not actual damage.

q: A Mac user is asked for a 'login keychain password' repeatedly after changing their account password via an admin reset. The fix is
options: Update the keychain password to match (or create a fresh login keychain); the keychain still uses the OLD password
explain: Admin password resets don't change the keychain's password, causing endless prompts until they're resynced.

q: A Mac spins the beachball for minutes whenever Finder opens a certain folder. Likely causes include
options: The Mac is too old to open folders
A huge folder of media generating previews, a failing drive, or a stuck network volume; test with a new folder and check Disk Utility
explain: Finder hangs usually trace to preview generation, dying disks, or unreachable network mounts.

q: AirDrop can't see any devices though Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are on. The setting to check is
options: AirDrop discovery is set to Everyone (or Contacts Only with the contact present) and no VPN/firewall is blocking it
explain: Discovery off (Receiving Off) is the most common cause, followed by restrictive contacts settings.

q: Time Machine reports 'backup disk not available' for a network backup. The checks are
options: Confirm the Mac is on the right network, the NAS/share is reachable, and re-select the disk in Time Machine settings
explain: Network backup targets fail silently when the share moves or credentials change.

q: Safari won't load any sites though Chrome works on the same Mac. Focus on
options: Safari-specific state: clear website data, disable extensions, and check Safari's proxy/content blockers
explain: Browser-specific failures mean browser-specific state—extensions and cached data lead the list.

q: Chromebook Android apps keep crashing after an update. The common fixes are
options: Powerwash immediately as the only option
Update ChromeOS and the Play Store components, clear the app's cache, or remove/reinstall the app
explain: Android container/app mismatches after updates usually yield to cache clears and component updates.

q: A Chromebook is 'slow' with everything lagging. The most common real cause is
options: Too many open tabs/extensions exhausting limited RAM; check the built-in task manager (Search+Esc)
explain: On low-RAM Chromebooks, tab/extension sprawl is the top performance complaint.

q: A user's ChromeOS profile shows 'profile error occurred' at sign-in. The typical resolution is
options: Remove the user from the device and add them again (their cloud data resyncs)
Call Google to delete the account
explain: Corrupt local profiles are disposable on ChromeOS because everything meaningful lives in the cloud account.

q: Windows CLOCK_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT blue screens point to
options: A CPU core not responding: check overclocks, BIOS/firmware, chipset drivers, and CPU power/thermals
explain: This stop code means a processor failed to respond to an interrupt—firmware/overclock/power are prime suspects.

q: IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL blue screens are most often caused by
options: A buggy (usually third-party) driver accessing paged memory at too high an IRQL
explain: This classic code fingers drivers; the minidump's stack usually names the .sys file.

q: MEMORY_MANAGEMENT blue screens direct the technician to
options: Test the RAM (Windows Memory Diagnostic/MemTest86) and check recent driver changes
explain: As the name says: memory (hardware or a driver corrupting it) is the first suspect.

q: DRIVER_POWER_STATE_FAILURE occurs typically when
options: A device/driver mishandles a sleep/wake power transition; update the offending device's driver
explain: Sleep/resume crashes with this code are driver power-management bugs.

q: VIDEO_TDR_FAILURE means
options: The GPU driver stopped responding and Windows' Timeout Detection and Recovery could not revive it
explain: TDR failures suggest GPU driver instability, overheating, or failing graphics hardware.

q: To find which driver caused repeated blue screens, the technician enables and reads
options: Small memory dumps (Startup and Recovery settings), then analyzes them with WinDbg or WhoCrashed/BlueScreenView
explain: Minidumps preserve the crash stack; viewer tools translate them into the likely culprit driver.

q: Driver Verifier (verifier.exe) is used to
options: Stress-test drivers to provoke latent bugs into visible crashes that identify the bad driver
explain: Verifier deliberately pressures drivers; use it carefully—it can make a machine unbootable until disabled in Safe Mode.

q: A game crashes with DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_HUNG after a GPU driver update. The standard remedy is
options: Clean-install the previous stable GPU driver (Display Driver Uninstaller in Safe Mode for a full clean)
explain: Corrupted driver remnants cause hangs; a clean rollback is the established cure.

q: CPU usage pegged at 100% by 'System Interrupts' suggests
options: A hardware device or its driver is flooding interrupts (DPC latency); update drivers and isolate the device
explain: Interrupt storms are hardware/driver-level; LatencyMon helps identify the guilty driver.

q: A laptop throttles heavily even while plugged in and set to High Performance. Beyond thermals, check
options: The OEM performance mode (vendor app/Fn key) and whether the correct-wattage adapter is in use
explain: Wrong/low-wattage adapters and 'quiet' OEM modes cap performance despite Windows settings.

q: FPS in games dropped sharply right after a Windows feature update. The likely fix path is
options: Update the GPU driver to a version supporting the new Windows build (and check Game Mode/fullscreen optimizations)
explain: Feature updates change the graphics stack (WDDM); matching drivers usually restore performance.

q: One application slowly consumes more and more RAM until the PC bogs down. This is
options: A memory leak in the app; restart it for relief and update/patch it for the fix (confirm via Task Manager/Performance over time)
explain: Unbounded growth over hours is the leak signature; only the vendor's fix is permanent.

q: Windows freezes completely at random intervals, requiring hard power-offs, with no blue screen. Prime suspects are
options: Failing storage, RAM errors, overheating, or PSU instability; check Reliability Monitor, temps, and drive health
explain: Hard hangs without BSOD skew toward hardware/power/thermal causes rather than a single driver.

q: BSOD 'CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED' after a cleanup tool ran suggests
options: Critical system files/registry were damaged; run DISM/SFC from WinRE and use System Restore if available
explain: Aggressive 'cleaners' delete needed components; image repair or restore is the recovery.

q: BSOD 'BAD_SYSTEM_CONFIG_INFO' most directly implicates
options: Corrupt registry hives (often after a bad shutdown or disk issue); System Restore/registry backup is the fix
explain: This code literally reports the configuration (registry) is damaged.

q: BSOD 'SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION' after installing new software usually means
options: The new software installed a faulty driver or service; uninstall it or roll back via Safe Mode
explain: Timing plus this code = a recently added kernel component misbehaving.

q: After enabling a Windows feature, install fails with error 0x800f081f. The cause/fix is
options: The component source wasn't found (WSUS lacks it); point DISM/Group Policy to installation media or allow Windows Update as the source
explain: 0x800f081f = source files not found, classic in WSUS-managed environments for Features on Demand.

q: Windows Update is stuck at 'Downloading 0%' for hours. Quick remedies include
options: Check for a metered connection, restart the Windows Update/BITS services, and confirm free disk space
explain: Metered links pause updates silently; stuck services and full disks are the other usual causes.

q: A feature update keeps failing and rolling back at the same percentage. The diagnostic tool built for this is
options: SetupDiag, which analyzes setup logs to identify the blocking driver/app/device
explain: SetupDiag parses Panther logs and reports the exact rollback cause.

q: A clean boot (MSConfig selective startup) is helping diagnose a conflict. The efficient method is
options: Binary search: disable half the third-party services/startup items, retest, and narrow down
explain: Halving the suspect set each round finds the culprit in a handful of reboots.

q: SFC reports it found corrupt files but 'was unable to fix some of them.' The details live in
options: The CBS.log (search for [SR] entries), after running DISM /RestoreHealth and SFC again
explain: CBS logging records every SFC verify/repair operation for manual follow-up.

q: An app installs fine but the Windows Sandbox fails to launch with a virtualization error. The fix is
options: Enable virtualization in BIOS/UEFI and the Virtual Machine Platform/Windows Hypervisor Platform features
explain: Sandbox needs hardware virtualization exposed plus its platform features turned on.

q: WSL fails to start with error 0x80370102. The meaning is
options: Virtualization is not enabled (BIOS setting and/or Virtual Machine Platform feature missing)
explain: 0x80370102 is WSL2's 'enable virtualization' error.

q: A Hyper-V VM has no network access after the host's NIC was replaced. The fix is
options: Rebind the external virtual switch to the new physical adapter (or recreate the vSwitch)
explain: External switches bind to a specific NIC; replacing it orphans the switch.

q: Quick Assist is the current Microsoft tool that replaced
options: Windows Remote Assistance for ad-hoc attended remote help (with the helper's Microsoft account)
explain: Quick Assist is the built-in, Store-delivered successor for helping another user interactively.

q: On Android, clearing an app's CACHE differs from clearing its DATA in that cache clearing
options: Removes temporary files only; clearing data resets the app completely (accounts, settings, databases)
explain: Cache first for glitches; data is the nuclear option that returns the app to first-run state.

q: An iPhone app keeps crashing after an update. 'Offload App' in storage settings helps because it
options: Removes the app binary but keeps its documents and data, then reinstalls a fresh copy
Deletes the app and its data permanently
Moves the app to iCloud forever
explain: Offload/reinstall refreshes a corrupt binary without losing the user's app data.

q: Android notifications for an important app arrive hours late. The usual cause is
options: Aggressive battery optimization (Doze/app standby) deferring the app; exempt it in battery settings
explain: Battery managers kill background work; whitelisting restores timely notifications (at some battery cost).

q: An iPhone user finds calls from unknown numbers go straight to voicemail. The feature responsible is likely
options: 'Silence Unknown Callers' (or a Focus mode filtering notifications)
explain: Silence Unknown Callers sends non-contact callers to voicemail automatically—users enable it and forget.

q: RCS messages on Android are stuck on 'Setting up…' or fall back to SMS. Common fixes are
options: Buy a new SIM every time
Update Carrier Services/messages app, verify the number, and toggle RCS off/on (or clear the app's data)
explain: RCS provisioning glitches clear with component updates and a re-registration cycle.

q: iMessage activation fails with 'waiting for activation' for days. The fix sequence includes
options: Confirm the phone number/Apple ID are correct, date/time is automatic, carrier SMS works, and toggle iMessage off/on
Replace the SIM as the only step
explain: Activation depends on a silent carrier SMS and correct time; the toggle forces a retry.

q: Android shows a 'Moisture detected' warning and blocks charging after the phone got slightly damp. Correct handling is
options: Blow a hair dryer on hot into the port
Let the port dry fully; do not override repeatedly or use rice myths as a fix—persistent false alerts need the port cleaned or serviced
explain: The sensor protects against shorts; most cases clear after drying. (Persistent false positives indicate corrosion/contamination.)

q: An iPhone displays 'Liquid detected in the Lightning connector' and refuses to charge. The user should
options: Use a metal pin to dry it
Disconnect, let it dry for several hours (emergency override exists but risks damage)
explain: iOS blocks charging to prevent corrosion/shorts; wireless charging can bridge the wait.

q: Auto-rotate stopped working on a phone after a drop; rotation lock is off. A diagnostic step is
options: Check the accelerometer in a diagnostics/sensor app; the sensor may be damaged
Factory reset as the only test
explain: Rotation depends on the accelerometer/gyroscope—drops kill sensors, and a sensor test isolates hardware.

q: One Bluetooth earbud is silent while the other plays. The common fixes are
options: Clean the mesh/contacts, check balance settings, and forget/re-pair the buds (resetting them in their case)
explain: Debris, balance sliders, and desynced bud pairing account for most one-sided audio.

q: A phone's GPS places the user a block away in every app. Improve accuracy by
options: Enabling high-accuracy location (Wi-Fi/Bluetooth scanning) and calibrating the compass (figure-8 motion)
explain: Assisted positioning from radios tightens fixes; magnetic interference throws the compass off.

q: Android alarms silently fail to fire for a user who relies on them. A leading cause is
options: The clock app is battery-optimized ('sleeping app'); exempt it, and check DND alarm settings
The ringtone is too quiet only
explain: OEM sleep lists aggressively suspend clock apps; exemption is the standard remedy.

q: iPhone Screen Time passcode is forgotten. The supported recovery is
options: Reset it using the Apple ID credentials used when Screen Time was set up
Restore from any backup file found online
There is no recovery; buy a new phone
explain: Since iOS 13.4, the Screen Time passcode resets via Apple ID verification.

q: An Android phone is stuck in a boot loop after an update. Before a factory reset, try
options: Wipe the cache partition from recovery mode (on models that support it)
Remove the battery while it loops (on sealed phones)
Keep it looping until the battery dies, then discard it
explain: A corrupt update cache causes many post-update loops; a cache wipe is non-destructive.

q: An iPhone is stuck on the Apple logo after an update. The correct first recovery is
options: Let the battery die for a week
Connect to a computer and use recovery mode to UPDATE (not Restore) iOS, preserving data
explain: Recovery-mode Update reinstalls iOS while keeping data; Restore (erasure) is the fallback.

q: After a factory reset, an Android phone demands the PREVIOUS owner's Google account. This is
options: Factory Reset Protection working as designed; only the prior account (or proof of purchase via the manufacturer/carrier) resolves it
explain: FRP is a theft deterrent; help desks must hand it back to the owner or follow the OEM proof-of-purchase process.

q: An eSIM transfer to a new phone fails repeatedly. The resolution path is
options: Reuse the same QR code indefinitely
Work with the carrier: they must issue a new eSIM activation/QR for the new device; old QR codes are single-use
explain: eSIM profiles are provisioned per device; carriers re-issue activation when transfers fail.

q: An Android work-profile user's camera is blocked 'by device policy.' The camera works in their personal profile. This is
options: Expected MDM policy behavior, not a fault; only the admin can change it
explain: Managed profiles enforce restrictions per-profile—the help desk answer is 'policy', escalated to the admin if wrong.

q: Google Play shows 'Download pending' for every app indefinitely. Fixes include
options: Cancel the stuck queue items, clear Play Store/Download Manager cache, and check storage space
explain: A single stuck download blocks the queue; clearing the store's cache restarts the pipeline.

q: An iOS update fails with 'Unable to Verify Update.' The common cure is
options: Delete the downloaded update in Storage and download it again on a stable network (and check storage space)
Set the date back a year
explain: Corrupted update packages fail verification; a fresh download fixes most cases.

q: A user's Android phone in Safe Mode works perfectly, but crashes return in normal mode. The conclusion is
options: A third-party app is causing the crashes; remove recently installed/updated apps
explain: Safe Mode disables third-party apps—stability there isolates the fault to an app.

q: An Android phone won't exit Safe Mode after a reboot. A frequent cause is
options: A stuck volume-down button (Safe Mode is triggered by holding it during boot), often from a case pressing it
explain: Debris or a tight case holding Volume Down reapplies Safe Mode at every boot.

q: Voicemail notifications won't clear on an Android phone even with no messages. The fix is
options: Clear the Phone app's data/cache (or have the carrier reset the mailbox indicator)
explain: Stuck MWI (message waiting indicator) clears with an app-data reset or carrier-side reset.

q: A dual-SIM user finds data comes out of the wrong (roaming) SIM after travel. The setting is
options: The default SIM for mobile data must be switched back in SIM manager settings
explain: Phones remember per-function SIM defaults; travel swaps often leave data on the travel SIM.

q: Calls on a phone sound fine, but the other party can't hear the user in ONE app while the phone app works. Check
options: That app's microphone permission (it was likely denied or revoked)
explain: Per-app mic permissions are the classic single-app audio failure.

q: A phone's screen brightness swings wildly indoors. Likely fix:
options: Clean the ambient light sensor area (often blocked by a case/screen protector) and reset adaptive brightness learning
explain: Adaptive brightness learns from a sensor that needs a clear view; protectors are frequent blockers.

q: A tablet pen (stylus) stopped working after the tablet's update. Checks include
options: Re-pair/reconnect the pen, confirm its battery/charge, and check for a pen-specific driver/firmware update
explain: Active pens are Bluetooth/battery devices with their own update path.

q: A managed iPad says 'This iPad is supervised and managed by…' and the user cannot remove an app. The help-desk answer is
options: Walk the user through deleting the profile
Tell them to erase the iPad
Correct: removal is restricted by the management profile; contact the organization's IT
It must be jailbroken to fix
explain: Supervised devices restrict profile changes by design; support should never coach a bypass.

q: A ChromeOS user's Linux apps suddenly won't launch after an update. A standard fix is
options: Update the Linux container (apt update/upgrade inside it) or remove and re-enable the Linux feature
explain: Container/host version drift breaks Crostini apps until the container is refreshed.

q: Windows users report the company VPN connects but internal sites won't load, while home sites work. A prime suspect is
options: Split-tunnel routing/DNS: internal DNS servers aren't being used for corporate names (suffix/NRPT issue)
The user's home router is too new
The sites are down for everyone
The VPN client needs a theme change
explain: Name resolution is the usual split-tunnel failure: traffic routes, but DNS answers come from the wrong place.

q: An RDP user gets 'An internal error has occurred' immediately on connect. Client-side fixes include
options: Clear the RDP bitmap cache (%localappdata%\Microsoft\Terminal Server Client) and reconnect; also test with NLA settings
explain: Corrupt client cache files are a well-known cause of instant RDP failures.

q: Outlook on the web works, but desktop Outlook says 'Trying to connect…' forever. A decisive test is
options: Create a new Outlook profile; if it connects, the old profile/Autodiscover cache is corrupt
explain: Profile corruption is the top cause of one-client connection failures.

q: A PDF form's fields are blank when opened on a phone, though the desktop shows entries. The explanation is
options: The phone's basic PDF viewer doesn't render the form layer (XFA/AcroForm) the same way; open in the full Acrobat app or flatten the form
explain: Viewer capability differences, not data loss—flattening (printing to PDF) bakes the values in.

q: A user edits a shared Excel file and their changes never appear for others, with no errors. Check whether
options: They are editing a local copy (from an email attachment or a synced placeholder) rather than the shared cloud file
The network is fine, so nothing is wrong
explain: 'Wrong copy' is the top silent collaboration failure—verify the file's location/path in the title bar.

q: Browser-based email works, but the mail app on a phone stopped syncing after the user changed their password. The fix is
options: The phone needs a new SIM
Update the password in the account settings or remove and re-add the account (token was invalidated)
explain: Password changes revoke app sessions; re-authenticating restores sync.

q: A smart TV app crashes on launch after a TV software update. Standard consumer fixes include
options: Power-cycle the TV fully (unplug 60 seconds), update/reinstall the app, or check the vendor's status
explain: Full power removal clears TV app caches that a remote 'off' doesn't.

q: A game console says NAT Type is 'Strict' and voice chat fails. The home-network fix is
options: Enable UPnP on the router or place the console in the router's DMZ/forward its ports (one console only for DMZ)
Turn off the router firewall entirely for all devices
explain: Strict NAT blocks peer connections; UPnP or port forwarding opens the needed paths.

q: A user's printer app on their phone finds no printers though the PC prints fine. The usual gap is
options: The phone is on a different network (guest Wi-Fi/VPN) or the printer lacks mobile print support (AirPrint/Mopria)
The phone needs a new battery
The PC is blocking it deliberately
explain: Discovery (mDNS) doesn't cross network segments; same-LAN is required.

q: Windows dictation (Win+H) and voice typing do nothing. Requirements to check are
options: A working microphone and an internet connection (voice typing is cloud-powered), plus language support for the display language
explain: Voice typing processes speech online and only for supported languages.

q: A user reports their screenshots suddenly save to OneDrive instead of Pictures. This is
options: OneDrive's folder backup (Known Folder Move) capturing the Screenshots/Pictures folder; adjust in OneDrive settings
explain: Known Folder Move redirects Pictures (including Screenshots) to OneDrive silently for many users.

q: A user double-clicks a .zip file and it opens in a photo app. The fix is
options: Change the default app for .zip (Settings > Default apps, or right-click > Open with > Always)
explain: Broken associations are per-extension; 'Open with > Always' repairs the specific one quickly.

q: ZIP folders won't open at all and the option to extract is missing after a third-party archiver was uninstalled. A fix is
options: Re-register the built-in ZIP handling (or reinstall an archiver); the uninstaller took the association/shell hooks with it
explain: Archivers register shell extensions; sloppy uninstalls orphan them.

q: Windows reports the Recycle Bin on C: is corrupted for EVERY user after a disk error. The deeper check is
options: Run chkdsk on the volume; recurring $Recycle.Bin corruption signals filesystem/disk problems
explain: One-off corruption is a folder fix; recurring corruption points at the disk itself.

q: A specific program always opens maximized off-screen on a phantom third monitor. A registry-free alternative fix is
options: Use Win+Shift+Left/Right arrows to move the window between displays
explain: The arrow shortcut teleports the focused window across displays.

q: Microsoft Store apps open to a blank window and close after a few seconds for one user. A repair that often works is
options: Clear the Store cache (wsreset) and re-register the Store package for that user
explain: Per-user package state again—cache and registration are the fault domain.

q: A user's Excel starts with a 'Personal.xlsb is locked for editing' prompt every time. The cause is
options: A leftover Excel process holding the personal macro workbook; end it in Task Manager (or delete the lock)
The file is on a read-only network forever
explain: Crashed Excel sessions leave the personal workbook locked by a ghost process.

q: Outlook takes 10 minutes 'Processing…' on the splash screen. A standard fix is
options: Start Outlook in Safe Mode (outlook /safe) to bypass add-ins, then disable the offending add-in; also check for a corrupt navigation pane (/resetnavpane)
Delete the OST as the only step
explain: Splash hangs are add-in/profile territory; /safe isolates, /resetnavpane repairs a classic corruption.

q: A user can't send email from Outlook: messages sit in the Outbox. Beyond connectivity, check
options: Whether an oversized attachment is wedged at the top of the Outbox (delete/move it offline) and that the account's outgoing server settings are right
explain: One huge stuck message blocks the queue behind it; Work Offline lets you remove it.

q: A shared mailbox doesn't automap in Outlook after being granted access yesterday. The mundane explanation is
options: Automapping/permission propagation can take time and an Outlook restart; also verify the permission type (Full Access automaps; Send As alone doesn't)
explain: Exchange permissions propagate on their own schedule; a restart and patience usually finish it.

q: Windows shows 'We can't sign in to your account' and loads a temporary profile after an update. The profile-repair step is
options: Check the ProfileList registry keys for a .bak entry and restore the correct profile path (after backing up the registry)
Ignore it; temp profiles are permanent
explain: The .bak ProfileList mix-up is the textbook cause; correcting the entries reunites the user with their profile.

q: A PC's fans spin up whenever it's idle, and Task Manager shows 'System Idle Process' at 99%. The user should be told
options: That's normal: System Idle Process percentage is time the CPU is doing NOTHING
A virus is mining at idle necessarily
explain: Idle Process is the accounting of free CPU, not a workload—a classic user misconception.

q: One drive letter vanished from Explorer though Disk Management shows the volume healthy. The quick check is
options: Whether the drive letter was removed (reassign it in Disk Management) or a policy/setting hides the drive
explain: Healthy-but-invisible volumes usually lost their letter or are hidden by the NoDrives setting.

q: A user's OneDrive icon vanished from the tray and sync stopped silently. Restart it by
options: Running OneDrive.exe (Win+R: %localappdata%\Microsoft\OneDrive\OneDrive.exe) and checking its startup entry
explain: OneDrive exits or loses its autostart after some updates; relaunching restores sync.

q: A corporate app fails only when the VPN is connected, working fine in the office. The pattern implicates
options: The app is allergic to homes
The VPN's DNS/routing for that app's servers (split tunnel missing a route) or MTU; not the app itself
The user's home PC is too old
explain: Location-dependent failure = path-dependent failure; the tunnel configuration is the variable.

q: Teams shows the user as 'Unknown user' / presence not updating. A known fix is
options: Clear the Teams cache (and sign out/in); new Teams stores cache under its package folder
explain: Presence/identity glitches in Teams are usually stale local cache.

q: Default browser keeps reverting to Edge after every update for one user. Beyond user choice, check
options: Whether a policy (GPO/MDM) or a 'browser protection' utility is enforcing the default
explain: Managed defaults come from policy or guard software that re-applies them.

q: A user gets 'The file is open in another program' for a local document no one else uses. The holder is often
options: The Explorer preview pane (or a crashed app instance) locking the file; close the preview/app process
explain: Preview handlers lock files for rendering; disabling the preview pane releases them.

q: Fonts appear jagged in Windows for one user after they 'optimized' settings. Restore via
options: ClearType Text Tuner (cttune) and the performance option 'Smooth edges of screen fonts'
explain: Users disable font smoothing in performance tweaks; ClearType recalibrates rendering.

q: The Windows key and taskbar shortcuts stop working while games run fine. A suspect is
options: The keyboard's 'game mode' or a stuck Win-Lock key disabling the Windows key
explain: Gaming keyboards have a Windows-key lock that's easy to trigger accidentally.

q: A user's second monitor works in Windows but the login screen appears only on the (closed) laptop lid. Set
options: The external display as the main display (or duplicate the screens) so sign-in shows where they look
explain: The sign-in screen follows the primary display designation.

q: Battery drains fast on a sleeping Windows laptop ('modern standby drain'). Diagnose with
options: powercfg /sleepstudy to see what kept the system active during standby
explain: SleepStudy reports the activators (network, devices, apps) behind standby drain.

q: Windows Hello works, but after undocking, face sign-in fails until reboot. A likely cause is
options: The dock's USB camera/IR path or a second camera confusing Hello; set the correct camera or restart the biometric service
explain: Multiple cameras (lid IR + dock webcam) confuse Hello's device selection.

q: An Excel add-in tab vanished after an Office update. The fix is
options: Re-enable the add-in in File > Options > Add-ins (check Disabled Items first)
explain: Crashes move add-ins to Disabled Items; they must be explicitly re-enabled there.

q: Word documents open in 'Protected View' from the local file server, annoying users. The correct admin fix is
options: Turn off Protected View for everything
Add the file server's location to Trusted Locations/trusted sites rather than disabling Protected View globally
explain: Trust the source location, not the whole internet-facing surface.

q: A user renamed their PC and now a mapped application that referenced the old name fails. The lesson/fix is
options: Update the app's server reference to the new name (or DNS alias); shortcuts/configs using the old hostname broke
Reinstall the app on every PC
explain: Name-based references break on renames—aliases (CNAME) prevent recurrence.

q: Linux: after editing /etc/fstab badly, the system boots to emergency mode. The fix path is
options: Use the emergency shell to remount root read-write, correct or comment the bad fstab line, and reboot
explain: A bad fstab entry halts the boot; emergency mode exists precisely for this repair.

q: Linux: a service fails at boot with 'address already in use.' The diagnostic is
options: ss -tulpn (or netstat) to find which process already holds the port
explain: Port conflicts are resolved by identifying the squatter process, not by blind restarts.

q: macOS: an external drive 'cannot be unmounted' when ejecting. The usual holder is
options: An app or process using the drive (Finder previews, Spotlight indexing, an open file); check with lsof or quit the app
explain: Spotlight indexing removable media is a classic eject blocker (can be excluded in Privacy settings).

q: macOS: Wi-Fi shows 'No hardware installed' after a software update. A known remedy sequence is
options: Reset NVRAM and the SMC (Intel) / restart (Apple silicon), and check System Information for the Wi-Fi interface
Buy a USB Wi-Fi dongle as the only fix
explain: Controller resets revive interfaces that vanish after updates.

q: Android: 'App not installed' when sideloading an update to an existing app. The classic cause is
options: Signature mismatch: the new APK is signed with a different key than the installed app (uninstall first, losing data)
explain: Android refuses cross-signature updates as a security measure.

q: Android: photos taken are not appearing in the gallery app. The media-store fix is
options: Clear the Media Storage app's data to force a rescan (or use a media-rescan), after confirming the files exist
explain: A corrupt media database hides existing files from gallery views.

q: iOS: 'Cannot connect to App Store' on one device while others work. A quick classic fix is
options: Check date/time (set automatically), sign out/in of the App Store, and toggle Wi-Fi
explain: Wrong clocks break store TLS handshakes just like browsers.

q: iOS: Mail shows 'Cannot Get Mail — connection to server failed' only on cellular. The setting is
options: Cellular data is turned off for the Mail app in Settings > Cellular
explain: Per-app cellular toggles silently cut apps off data while Wi-Fi works.
