q: ChromeOS: the shelf and launcher freeze after sign-in. A common fix is
options: Sign in as Guest to test; if fine, remove/re-add the user profile (cloud data resyncs)
explain: Guest isolation separates profile corruption from system faults on ChromeOS too.

q: A Windows user's 'Send to > Mail recipient' does nothing. The cause is
options: No default MAPI mail client is set (or the default app for email is a store app that doesn't register MAPI)
The file is too large to attach ever
explain: Send To uses MAPI; a missing/unregistered default client breaks it silently.

q: PDFs print with a black background (white text invisible) from one PC. The likely setting is
options: Windows is in dark mode permanently
The reader is printing in a 'print as image'/accessibility color replacement mode or the driver is set to negative; check print settings and driver color options
explain: Accessibility document-color overrides and driver settings can invert output on one machine only.

q: An ESD strap protects components by
options: Grounding the component to the building's water pipes
Insulating the technician from the bench
Removing all static from the room permanently
Keeping the technician and the work at the same electrical potential so no static discharge occurs
explain: Equal potential means no voltage difference—and no spark—between you and the part.

q: You should NOT wear an ESD strap when working inside
options: Power supplies and CRT monitors, because of stored high-voltage charge and shock risk
explain: Inside PSUs/CRTs the danger is lethal stored charge; isolation, not grounding, is the safety rule there.

q: Storing a removed motherboard correctly means placing it
options: On top of the PC case
In a regular plastic grocery bag
explain: Shielding bags form a Faraday cage; plain plastic builds static.

q: Low humidity environments increase ESD risk because
options: Dry air doesn't dissipate static charges, so they build up to higher voltages
explain: Humid air bleeds charge away; winter-dry rooms are peak ESD season.

q: A Safety Data Sheet (SDS) must be consulted before
options: Using a chemical cleaner or solvent, to learn its hazards, PPE, and spill response
explain: SDS documents (formerly MSDS) are the legal source for chemical hazards and first aid.

q: Class C fires involve
options: Energized electrical equipment; extinguish with CO2 or dry chemical—never water while energized
explain: Water conducts electricity back to the operator; Class C requires non-conductive agents (and cutting power first).

q: The PASS technique for fire extinguishers stands for
explain: PASS is the standard extinguisher operation taught in workplace safety.

q: Before opening a power supply (which should generally not be serviced), the critical hazard is
options: Capacitors can hold a lethal charge long after unplugging—PSUs are replace-don't-repair for field techs
explain: Field procedure is to replace PSUs whole; internal repair is for qualified electronics benches.

q: Removing rings, watches, and dangling jewelry before working in equipment protects against
options: Electrical shorts and getting caught in moving parts
explain: Metal jewelry bridges circuits and snags fans and drives.

q: A GFCI outlet protects people by
options: Tripping in milliseconds when current leaks to ground (e.g., through a person)
explain: Ground-fault interrupters compare outgoing/returning current and cut power on imbalance.

q: Removing the third (ground) prong from a plug is dangerous because it
options: Defeats the equipment's fault protection, leaving the chassis able to become live
explain: The ground pin is a safety path for fault current; adapters that defeat it create shock hazards.

q: Daisy-chaining power strips is prohibited because
options: It overloads circuits and strips, creating a fire hazard (and violates fire code in workplaces)
Strips cancel each other's surge protection magically
explain: Each strip is rated for a load; chaining multiplies outlets beyond the wiring's safe capacity.

q: When racking servers, the heaviest equipment goes
options: At the bottom of the rack for stability (with anti-tip measures for tall racks)
explain: Low center of gravity prevents tip-overs when units slide out on rails.

q: Hot aisle/cold aisle layouts improve data center cooling by
options: Keeping server intakes facing cold aisles and exhausts facing hot aisles so air streams don't mix
Reducing the need for CRAC units entirely
explain: Containment of hot/cold air raises cooling efficiency and prevents hot spots.

q: Typical recommended data-center conditions per ASHRAE guidance center on
options: About 18-27°C (64-81°F) inlet temperatures with controlled humidity
explain: Modern ASHRAE envelopes are warmer than the old 'meat locker' rooms, saving energy safely.

q: Positive air pressure in a server room helps by
options: Pushing air out through cracks so dust and contaminants are kept out when doors open
explain: Slight overpressure plus filtration keeps the room cleaner.

q: Water leak sensors under raised floors and near CRAC units exist because
options: They are required for the fire panel
Undetected leaks destroy equipment and cabling long before they're visible
explain: Early leak detection under the floor prevents catastrophic water damage.

q: Spent lithium and lead-acid batteries must be disposed of by
options: Recycling through approved battery/e-waste channels—never regular trash or incineration
explain: Batteries contain hazardous materials and fire risks; regulations mandate recycling streams.

q: Used toner cartridges should be
options: Returned through the manufacturer's recycling program (or an e-waste handler), not landfilled
explain: Vendor take-back programs exist for nearly every cartridge; toner powder is a respiratory irritant.

q: A CRT monitor requires special disposal because
options: It contains leaded glass and a vacuum tube that can implode—handled as hazardous e-waste
It is too heavy for trash trucks
explain: CRTs carry pounds of lead; jurisdictions ban them from landfills.

q: A swollen lithium battery in a laptop brought to the help desk should be
options: Charged to see if it improves
Put in the regular trash if it still works
Not charged or punctured; power off, isolate the device in a fire-resistant area, and follow hazardous handling/disposal procedure
explain: Swollen cells are damaged and can vent/fire; handle as a safety incident, not a repair.

q: If a user spills liquid into a running desktop, the first action is
options: Turn it upside down while running
Keep working to save files first
Cut power immediately (unplug), then assess—electricity and liquid are the urgent danger
Blow it dry with a hair dryer while plugged in
explain: De-energize first; data concerns come after the shock/short risk is gone.

q: For cleaning electrical contacts and boards, the appropriate solvent is
options: High-percentage (90%+) isopropyl alcohol, which evaporates cleanly
explain: IPA dissolves flux/oils and flashes off without leaving conductive residue.

q: Screens should be cleaned with
options: A microfiber cloth lightly dampened with water or screen-safe cleaner—never spray liquid directly onto the display
Paper towels and ammonia glass cleaner
explain: Direct spraying seeps into bezels; ammonia damages coatings; paper fibers scratch.

q: Only ESD-safe vacuums should be used inside equipment because
options: They have better filters for toner only
They are required to be red
Ordinary vacuums generate large static charges at the nozzle that can kill components
explain: Standard vacuum hoses are static generators; ESD-safe models use conductive paths.

q: Compressed air cleaning should be done with
options: The can inverted for extra cold on chips
Short bursts, can upright, fans held still, ideally outdoors or away from the workspace (blown dust goes somewhere)
While the system is running and open on the user's desk
explain: Inverted cans spray freezing liquid propellant; long blasts overspin fans and spread dust through the office.

q: The ozone and fine toner dust produced by laser printers mean they should be placed
options: In ventilated areas, not sealed small offices where people sit all day
Next to the CEO's desk for status
explain: Printers emit ultrafine particles; ventilation and distance are the standard controls.

q: You smell burnt electronics from a PC. The correct response is
options: Power it off and unplug it, keep it off, and investigate before any further power-on
Keep using it if it still works
Open it while running to look
Spray it with a fire extinguisher immediately in all cases
explain: A component is actively failing; continued power risks fire and further damage.

q: Working inside a PC that must be plugged in for a measurement, the 'one-hand rule' reduces
options: The chance of current crossing the chest/heart (keep one hand out of the equipment)
explain: One-hand-in technique plus an isolation transformer is classic live-work safety.

q: Cable runs across walkways are both a trip hazard and an equipment risk; the correct fix is
options: Route them in cable raceways/covers or overhead/underfloor paths, never loose tape as a permanent solution
Run more cables to average the risk
explain: Cable protectors and proper pathways are the code-compliant remedies.

q: Team lifting (or a lift tool) is required when
options: Equipment exceeds safe solo lifting weight (commonly ~50 lbs/23 kg) or is awkward—servers and UPS units qualify
explain: UPS units and 2U servers are dense and awkward; lifts prevent back injuries.

q: Proper monitor ergonomics place the screen
options: About an arm's length away, with the top of the screen at or slightly below eye level
Above eye level to look up
explain: Correct height/distance prevents neck and eye strain over long shifts.

q: The 20-20-20 rule for eye strain says
options: Every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds
explain: Regular distance refocusing relaxes the ciliary muscle and reduces digital eye strain.

q: Repetitive strain injury prevention at a desk includes
options: A wrist rest used while actively typing
Neutral wrist position, elbows near 90°, feet flat, and regular micro-breaks to move
explain: Posture plus movement breaks are the evidence-based RSI controls.

q: Before drilling or mounting access points/cameras in ceilings, coordinate to check for
options: Hidden hazards: electrical runs, plumbing, asbestos in older buildings, and plenum requirements
explain: Ceiling work intersects building systems and regulated materials—asbestos checks are mandatory in older sites.

q: Ladder and height work for installs should follow
options: Your organization's safety policy: correct ladder type/rating, three points of contact, and a second person for overhead work
Standing on the top rung for reach
Working alone at night to avoid bother
explain: Falls are a leading workplace injury; installs don't exempt technicians.

q: Confined spaces (attics, crawl spaces, raised-floor plenums) require
options: A partner waiting outside only if convenient
Awareness of entry rules and hazards; never enter a permit-required confined space without the proper program
explain: Technicians regularly face these spaces pulling cable; knowing the boundaries keeps them safe.

q: A first responder finding an unconscious coworker near electrical equipment should
options: Pull them away immediately by hand
Not touch them until power is cut (shock risk), then call emergency services and begin aid if safe
explain: The victim may still be in contact with a live source—scene safety comes first.

q: Emergency evacuation during a fire alarm means
options: Leave by the nearest safe exit, do not use elevators, do not stop for equipment or data
Use the elevator to save time
explain: Life safety outranks all equipment; alarms are treated as real.

q: An AED in the workplace is used for
options: Delivering a guided defibrillation shock for sudden cardiac arrest—it talks the rescuer through it
explain: AEDs are designed for lay rescuers with voice prompts; early defibrillation saves lives.

q: Workplace incidents and near-misses should be
options: Only reported if someone is hospitalized
Reported promptly per policy—even when no one was hurt—so hazards get corrected
explain: Near-miss reporting is how organizations fix dangers before injuries.

q: Chemical splashes in the eyes require
options: Waiting to see if it improves
Immediate eyewash station flushing (15 minutes) and medical evaluation
explain: Eyewash first, questions later—chemical eye injuries are time-critical.

q: The correct order of priorities in any workplace emergency is
options: People first, then environment/facilities, then equipment and data
explain: Every emergency procedure on the A+ objectives puts life safety ahead of assets.

q: Gloves worn when handling toner or cleaning inside printers protect against
options: Chemical exposure and sharp internal edges (and keep oils off sensitive parts)
explain: Nitrile gloves are standard PPE for printer internals and chemical handling.

q: Hearing protection becomes relevant for IT staff when
options: Working for extended periods in loud environments like data centers with high-decibel cooling
explain: Data center noise can exceed safe prolonged-exposure levels; facilities provide protection.

q: Good housekeeping in a tech work area (bench discipline) prevents
options: Lost screws/parts, ESD events from clutter, and accidental damage—parts organized, liquids away from equipment
explain: An organized bench is both a safety and a quality control.

q: When moving a rack-mounted UPS, remember that
options: It can be carried by its front handles alone safely
It is extremely heavy for its size (batteries) and may need batteries removed or a lift; plan the move
It weighs the same as a server
It must stay plugged in while moving
explain: Lead-acid batteries make UPS units deceptively heavy—many injuries happen here.

q: A formal change management process exists primarily to
options: Evaluate, approve, schedule, and document changes so risks are controlled and outages are minimized
Slow down all work as much as possible
Let anyone change anything if they document it later
explain: Change control balances speed with risk: assessment, approval, communication, implementation, and review.

q: A standard change differs from a normal change in that a standard change is
options: Pre-approved, low-risk, and repeatable (it follows a documented procedure)
explain: Standard changes (e.g., password-policy-approved routine tasks) skip per-instance CAB approval.

q: An emergency change is handled by
options: An expedited approval path (ECAB/on-call authority) with documentation completed afterward, used only for urgent fixes
explain: Emergencies compress—not eliminate—the process; retrospective documentation is mandatory.

q: Every significant change plan should include a rollback (back-out) plan that defines
options: Who to blame if it fails
How to return to the previous state, and the decision point/criteria for invoking it
explain: No rollback plan, no approval: failed changes without an exit path become outages.

q: A change freeze window is typically declared
options: During critical business periods (fiscal close, peak retail, audits) when only emergency changes are allowed
When the CAB is on vacation
explain: Freezes protect the business when change risk is least affordable.

q: Testing a change in a non-production environment first accomplishes
options: Doubling the work for no reason
Validation of the procedure and discovery of side effects without business impact
explain: Dev/test validation is where most change failures should happen.

q: The Change Advisory Board (CAB) is responsible for
options: Assessing the risk, impact, and scheduling of significant changes and recommending approval or rejection
explain: The CAB advises; the change manager owns the final decision and schedule.

q: A post-implementation review (PIR) asks
options: Did the change achieve its goal, cause incidents, and what should be learned or improved
How to skip CAB next time
explain: PIRs close the loop—especially after failed or incident-causing changes.

q: The most common cause of change-related outages is
options: Untested or poorly understood changes (and changes made outside the process)
explain: Industry post-mortems consistently blame inadequate testing and unauthorized changes.

q: Good ticket documentation includes
options: The user's password for next time
Symptoms, environment, steps tried, root cause, resolution, and verification—written so another tech could reproduce the fix
explain: Tickets are the organization's memory; future incidents depend on their quality.

q: Passwords and secrets must never be written in tickets because
options: Tickets are broadly readable and retained; secrets belong in a vault/password manager
explain: Storing credentials in tickets is a recurring breach source.

q: An asset register (inventory) should track at minimum
options: Asset tag/serial, assigned user, location, purchase date/cost, warranty, and lifecycle status
explain: Accurate inventory underpins support, refresh planning, audits, and disposal.

q: Asset lifecycle stages in order are
explain: Lifecycle management ensures refreshes, warranty use, and secure disposal happen on schedule.

q: A CMDB (Configuration Management Database) stores
options: Configuration items and their relationships (which server runs which service depends on which database)
explain: The CMDB's relationship map is what makes impact analysis of changes possible.

q: Labeling both ends of every cable run pays off because
options: Any cable can be traced instantly during troubleshooting and moves, without tone tools or guesswork
explain: Consistent labeling standards are among the cheapest reliability investments in a facility.

q: Network documentation should include, at minimum
options: Just a list of user names
Logical and physical diagrams, IP address management (IPAM), VLANs, and provider circuit details
explain: When the network is down, the documentation is the map—stale diagrams are worse than none.

q: A knowledge base article is most valuable when it
options: Captures a verified fix in searchable, step-by-step form so anyone can resolve the issue next time
Contains the author's opinions on users
explain: KBs convert one technician's hard-won fix into organizational capability.

q: Software license compliance matters because
options: Using more copies than licensed exposes the organization to audits, fines, and forced true-up purchases
explain: License audits are routine; a license register with entitlements vs. deployments is the defense.

q: A per-device license differs from a per-user license in that it
options: Licenses the machine regardless of who uses it; per-user licenses follow the person across their devices
explain: Choosing the right metric (user/device/core/concurrent) dramatically changes cost and compliance.

q: Concurrent-use licensing allows
options: As many installs as wanted, as long as simultaneous users don't exceed the licensed count
explain: Floating licenses suit shared tools (e.g., CAD) used by rotating staff.

q: An open-source license such as the GPL can affect a business because
options: Distributing software that incorporates GPL code can require releasing source under the same terms
It makes all software free of obligations
explain: Copyleft obligations are real: legal review is needed before embedding GPL components in distributed products.

q: Subscription (SaaS) licensing shifts the admin's job toward
options: Tracking seats, renewals, and actual usage so the company doesn't overpay or lapse
explain: Shelfware (unused seats) and surprise lapses are the SaaS-era license risks.

q: A EULA's most practically important clauses for IT cover
options: Installation/transfer rights, device/user counts, and virtualization rights
explain: Transfer and VM rights decide whether imaging and VDI deployments are compliant.

q: Volume licensing programs (e.g., Microsoft) typically require tracking
options: Product keys/activations centrally (KMS/MAK counts) and retaining proof of purchase for audits
explain: Proof of entitlement is what an audit actually examines.

q: When software is uninstalled from a retired PC, the license should be
options: Reclaimed into the license pool for redeployment, per its terms
explain: Harvesting licenses from retired assets is a major cost saver—and auditors check the trail.

q: An Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) defines
options: What employees may and may not do with company systems, networks, and data
explain: The AUP is the behavioral contract; violations are HR matters backed by this signed document.

q: Employees typically acknowledge the AUP
options: At hire and whenever it materially changes (with records kept)
explain: Signed acknowledgments are what make enforcement defensible.

q: Prohibited activities under most AUPs include
options: Running personal businesses on company systems, illegal downloading, and bypassing security controls
Using the printer for a boarding pass once
explain: AUPs ban conduct that creates legal/security exposure, not ordinary work.

q: Handling a policy violation you witness follows
options: Your organization's escalation path (document facts, notify the appropriate authority)—not personal confrontation or snooping
Investigating the coworker's personal files yourself
Posting about it on social media
explain: Technicians report through channels; freelance investigations create legal problems.

q: Documentation in tickets must be
options: Written to make the writer look good
Objective and factual—no blame, speculation, or derogatory remarks (tickets are discoverable records)
explain: Tickets surface in audits, lawsuits, and customer disputes; write them accordingly.

q: PII appearing in a ticket (screenshots, logs) should be
options: Emailed to the team for awareness
Minimized/redacted where possible and handled per privacy policy
explain: Tickets are long-lived; unnecessary PII inside them is a compliance liability.

q: An SLA's 'response time' and 'resolution time' differ in that response means
options: Acknowledging and beginning work on the ticket; resolution means the issue is actually fixed
explain: SLAs usually bind both: first response within X, resolution within Y, by priority.

q: Ticket priority is normally set by
options: Impact × urgency (how many people/how critical, and how time-sensitive)
explain: Priority matrices keep emotion out of triage.

q: An escalation is appropriate when
options: The issue exceeds your access, skills, or timebox—or breaches SLA thresholds
explain: Escalation is a designed pathway, not a failure—with a warm handoff and full notes.

q: A proper shift handoff note contains
options: Open issues, their current state, what's been tried, next steps, and any time-critical deadlines
explain: Continuity failures at handoffs are a top cause of dropped incidents.

q: During a major incident, stakeholder communication should be
options: Regular and scheduled (e.g., every 30-60 minutes), factual about impact, actions, and next update time—even if there's no fix yet
explain: 'No update' updates prevent rumor spirals and executive escalations.

q: An after-action review (postmortem) should be
options: Blameless and focused on systemic causes and corrective actions with owners and deadlines
A search for who to punish
Skipped if the outage was short
explain: Blameless reviews produce honest timelines; blame produces hidden facts.

q: Remote support sessions should begin with
options: Opening their files to look around first
Announcing yourself, explaining what you'll do, and obtaining the user's consent before taking control
explain: Consent and narration protect the user and the technician.

q: While remotely connected, a technician should never
options: Browse the user's personal files or photos unrelated to the issue
explain: Curiosity browsing is a policy and ethics violation, and often logged.

q: Vendor escalation works best when you provide
options: Model/serial numbers, firmware versions, exact symptoms, what you've already tried, and logs—before the call
explain: Front-loading facts skips the scripted first tier and shortens resolution.

q: An RMA shipment for a failed drive containing sensitive data should follow
options: Data-destruction/retention policy first—some vendors offer keep-your-drive options; never ship readable sensitive media against policy
Formatting it once and assuming safety
Including the admin password in the box
explain: Warranty returns are a classic data-leak path; policy governs whether media may leave.

q: Configuration drift is dangerous because
options: It is always the user's fault
Systems silently diverge from their documented/secured state, breaking troubleshooting assumptions and security baselines
explain: Drift is why 'works on the identical server' stops being true.

q: Naming conventions for devices/accounts matter operationally because
options: Consistent, meaningful names make logs, alerts, and tickets unambiguous across the whole team
explain: A name that encodes site/type/role (e.g., NYC-SRV-DB02) accelerates every conversation about it.

q: A 'runbook' differs from general documentation in that it
options: Gives exact step-by-step responses to specific operational situations (alerts, failures) an on-call tech can execute at 3 AM
explain: Runbooks are procedures under pressure: precise, tested, and current.

q: When a procedure document and reality disagree, the technician should
options: Follow the safe/correct course and then get the document corrected through its owner—never quietly ignore it forever
Always follow the document even if wrong
Blame the author in the ticket
explain: Documents improve only when practitioners feed corrections back.

q: Backups of documentation itself matter because
options: During the worst incidents (network/storage down), you need offline access to diagrams, contacts, and runbooks
explain: The DR binder (printed/ offline copies) exists because the wiki dies with the network.

q: The GFS backup rotation scheme stands for
options: Grandfather-Father-Son: daily (son), weekly (father), and monthly (grandfather) media sets with increasing retention
explain: GFS gives layered retention points while reusing media efficiently.

q: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) defines
options: The maximum acceptable time to restore a service after a disaster
How much data loss is acceptable
The time to detect an incident
explain: RTO is about time-to-restore; RPO is about acceptable data loss (how far back you rewind).

q: If a business sets an RPO of 4 hours, backups/replication must
options: Run at least every 4 hours, so at most 4 hours of data is lost
explain: RPO drives backup frequency: the interval between recovery points cannot exceed it.

q: A hot site differs from a warm site in that a hot site
options: Has hardware but no current data
Is just empty space with power
Is fully equipped and running with current data, ready for immediate failover
explain: Hot = live duplicate (minutes), warm = equipment ready needing data restore (hours), cold = space/utilities only (days).

q: Tabletop DR exercises test
options: The plan and people: walking through scenarios verbally to find gaps, without touching systems
explain: Tabletops are cheap, frequent, and expose missing contacts/steps before a real disaster does.

q: Single points of failure are eliminated by
options: Identifying components whose lone failure kills a service and adding redundancy for them
explain: SPOF analysis drives targeted redundancy: power, storage, network paths, people knowledge.

q: Restore priority after a disaster should follow
options: The business impact analysis: revenue/safety-critical services first, in dependency order
explain: The BIA ranks services by business impact; dependencies (identity/DNS before apps) set the sequence.

q: Backup failure alerts must be acted on promptly because
options: Silent backup failures are usually discovered during the disaster they're meant to protect against
explain: Reviewing backup reports daily is a core operational duty.

q: Seeding an initial cloud backup for a large site usually involves
options: Uploading 20 TB over the office DSL on day one
Shipping an encrypted drive/device to the provider for the first bulk upload, then syncing changes
explain: Seed devices solve the first-full-backup bandwidth problem.

q: Backup encryption keys must be
options: Stored separately from the backups (escrowed) so a restore is possible when primary systems are gone
Kept only on the backup server
The same as the admin password, written on the tape
explain: Encrypted backups without reachable keys are indistinguishable from no backups.

q: Cloud backup restores of entire servers can be slow/expensive mainly due to
options: Download bandwidth and egress fees; plan RTOs around them or keep local copies for fast restores
explain: Egress realities shape hybrid designs: local for speed, cloud for disaster.

q: PCI DSS applies to organizations that
options: Store, process, or transmit payment card data; it mandates controls like encryption, access control, and logging
explain: Any business taking cards is in scope; the cardholder data environment must be segmented and controlled.

q: Under HIPAA, a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) is required when
options: A vendor will handle protected health information (PHI) on behalf of a healthcare organization
explain: No BAA, no PHI sharing: cloud providers must sign one before hosting health data.

q: GDPR grants individuals rights including
options: Access to their personal data, correction, and erasure ('right to be forgotten'), with breach notification duties for controllers
explain: GDPR's reach covers any organization handling EU residents' personal data.

q: Data retention policies must balance
options: Keeping data as long as legally/business-required—and no longer—against storage cost and breach exposure
explain: Over-retention is its own risk: breached archives of data you didn't need are indefensible.

q: When a data breach is suspected, employees' first duty is
options: Post about it internally on chat for awareness first
Reimage the machine to clean it
Report immediately through the incident channel and preserve evidence—do not investigate solo or delete anything
Wait to see if it spreads
explain: Speed and preservation beat curiosity; the IR plan depends on both.

q: Patch SLAs are commonly tiered so that
options: All patches wait for the annual cycle
Critical vulnerabilities are remediated fastest (e.g., days), with longer windows for lower severities
explain: Severity-based timelines balance exploitation risk against change risk.

q: A staged (ring-based) patch/software rollout reduces risk by
options: Deploying to a small pilot group first, then progressively wider rings after validation
explain: Rings contain bad releases to a few machines instead of the fleet.

q: If a deployed patch breaks a business app fleet-wide, the operational response is
options: Wait for the next Patch Tuesday
Execute the rollback: uninstall the patch via management tooling and pause its deployment ring, then document
explain: Management platforms can mass-uninstall; pausing the ring stops further spread.

q: WSUS/Intune approval workflows exist so that
options: Administrators control which updates deploy and when, instead of every machine pulling from Microsoft unmanaged
explain: Approvals enforce testing and scheduling discipline in managed fleets.

q: Before a fleet-wide OS upgrade, compatibility readiness includes
options: Just sending the upgrade at night
Inventorying critical apps/hardware, testing them on the new OS, and piloting with representative users
Upgrading the CEO first without telling them
explain: App-compat surprises are the #1 cause of failed OS migrations.

q: Driver strategy during OS imaging should be
options: Maintain a tested driver store per model in the deployment system; don't let Windows Update gamble during builds
Use one universal driver pack for everything forever
Skip drivers and let users install them
explain: Model-based driver injection keeps images clean and builds predictable.

q: Go-live support for a major rollout should include
options: The whole IT team on vacation
Removing the old system instantly with no fallback
Floor-walkers/extra help-desk coverage and a known-issues list for the first days
explain: Hypercare catches the predictable surge and builds user confidence.

q: Users resist a new system less when IT provides
options: Advance communication about why/when, short role-based training, and easy help channels
explain: Change adoption is an operational deliverable, not an afterthought.

q: Screen-lock timeout policies are typically enforced at
options: Around 5-15 minutes of inactivity for office workstations (shorter in sensitive areas)
explain: Auto-lock balances security ( unattended sessions) against usability; sensitive zones go shorter.

q: New-hire IT provisioning should follow
options: A checklist tied to HR's start notice: accounts, hardware, access per role, and training—ready on day one
Giving everyone the previous person's setup and passwords
Waiting for the hire to ask for each thing
explain: Checklists make onboarding consistent and auditable—and day-one readiness is IT's reputation.

q: An employee departure IT checklist must include
options: Deleting their mailbox immediately before HR confirms
Disabling accounts at the agreed time, recovering equipment, transferring data ownership, and revoking tokens/keys
explain: Missed revocations (SaaS tokens, personal devices) are the common leaver risk.

q: Loaner equipment procedures protect the organization by
options: Letting staff borrow freely without records
Logging who has what, its condition, and return dates—with data wiped between loans
explain: Sign-out logs prevent 'lost' assets; wiping between users prevents data leakage.

q: Spare-parts (FRU) inventory should be managed with
options: Minimum stock levels for failure-prone parts (drives, PSUs, fans, batteries) based on fleet size and lead times
No spares; next-day shipping always suffices
explain: Right-sized spares turn multi-day outages into same-day repairs.

q: Shipping equipment for repair/return should use
options: Original or equivalent protective packaging, anti-static protection, insurance, and tracking—documented in the ticket
explain: Transit damage and lost shipments are prevented by boring packaging discipline.

q: Color-coding network cables by function (e.g., blue=LAN, yellow=WAN, red=crossover/management) helps by
options: Making the plant readable at a glance—when the convention is documented and followed consistently
explain: Color is a fast visual index, but it supplements—never replaces—labels.

q: Printer fleet management includes tracking
options: Toner/consumable levels with reorder thresholds, page counts, and error trends per device
explain: Consumable forecasting prevents the 'out of toner during payroll run' class of outage.

q: Test equipment like multimeters should be
options: Inspected before use and calibrated/replaced per schedule; damaged test leads are a shock hazard
Used on any voltage regardless of rating
explain: CAT ratings and lead condition determine whether a meter is safe for the circuit.

q: A preventative-maintenance schedule for workstations typically includes
options: Periodic dust cleaning, health checks (disk SMART), update verification, and cable/connection inspections
Annual reimaging of every PC regardless of need
explain: Light scheduled care prevents the most common age-related failures.

q: Standard operating procedures (SOPs) should be reviewed
options: By deleting old versions for juniors to rediscover
On a schedule and after incidents or process changes—owned by a named person
explain: Stale SOPs are worse than missing ones because people trust them.

q: Quality metrics for a help desk include
options: First-contact resolution rate, CSAT, mean time to resolve, and reopen rate
explain: Balanced metrics prevent gaming (closing fast but wrong).

q: After closing a ticket, a brief satisfaction follow-up serves to
options: Confirm the user is actually satisfied and catch silent failures before they become complaints
explain: Verification with the requester is part of the resolution, not paperwork.

q: A user insists a ticket be closed but the problem recurs weekly. The professional approach is
options: Reopen/link the incidents and escalate to a problem investigation rather than repeatedly closing quick fixes
Close it and ignore the pattern
Tell the user to live with it
explain: Recurring incidents signal a problem record/root cause, not seven coincidences.

q: Problem management differs from incident management in that problem management
options: Hunts the underlying cause of recurring incidents to prevent them permanently
explain: Incidents restore service; problems remove causes.

q: Knowledge gained from a problem investigation should end up
options: In the knowledge base and, where relevant, in changes to standards/images/procedures
explain: Institutional learning is the return on problem management.

q: Change, incident, and asset records are linked because
options: A change can cause incidents; incidents reference assets; the records together tell the whole story
explain: Linkage is what turns tickets into traceable operational history.

q: End-of-life (EOL) software must be tracked because
options: After EOL it receives no security patches; continued use needs isolation, replacement plans, or compensating controls
It stops working on the EOL date
explain: EOL systems (old Windows, Java, browsers) are standing vulnerabilities in audits.

q: An application inventory (software catalog) supports
options: Knowing what's installed where—for licensing, patching, vulnerability response, and standardization
explain: You cannot patch or license what you cannot enumerate.

q: Unsupported ('shadow') software discovered on a workstation should be
options: Left alone if the user likes it
Deleted with the user's files as punishment
Assessed, then approved-and-managed or removed per policy—documented either way
explain: The goal is a managed estate, not a raid.

q: Warranty status checks before repairing hardware save money because
options: In-warranty failures are the vendor's cost—and unauthorized self-repair can void coverage
explain: Always check entitlement first: serial number tells the story.

q: An out-of-band management system (e.g., iDRAC/iLO) helps operations by
options: Letting admins power-cycle, console into, and diagnose servers remotely even when the OS is down
explain: Lights-out management is why a 3 AM server hang doesn't require a drive to the office.

q: Time synchronization across logs matters operationally because
options: Correlating events between systems (firewall, server, badge reader) is impossible if their clocks disagree
explain: Incident timelines are built from logs; skew destroys them.

q: Documentation of root passwords/keys belongs in
options: A managed password vault with access logging—not in documents, tickets, or spreadsheets
A sticky note in the server room
explain: Vaulting with individual accountability is the only acceptable pattern.

q: Active listening during a support call means
options: Letting the user finish, paraphrasing their issue back, and asking clarifying questions before touching anything
Typing the ticket while they talk and ignoring details
Assuming you know the problem from the first word
explain: Most misdiagnoses come from solving the problem the tech imagined instead of the one described.

q: When a user explains a problem in non-technical language, the technician should
options: Use maximum jargon to sound expert
Tell them to Google the terms
Translate without condescension: confirm understanding in plain terms and avoid jargon (or explain it when needed)
explain: Meeting users at their level builds trust and gets accurate information.

q: Setting expectations at the start of a repair includes
options: Promising it will definitely be fixed in 10 minutes
What you'll do, roughly how long it may take, what could go wrong, and when you'll update them
Warning them it will probably break
explain: Honest framing prevents the frustration that silence and surprises create.

q: Before closing a ticket, the technician should
options: Close it as soon as your part is done
Confirm with the user that the issue is resolved and demonstrate/test the fix together
Let the auto-close timer handle it always
explain: User-verified resolution is what 'resolved' means.

q: A user is angry about a recurring outage. The professional response is to
options: Acknowledge the impact, apologize for the disruption, explain what's being done, and give a concrete follow-up time
Argue that it's not IT's fault
explain: De-escalation starts with empathy and ownership, not defense.

q: When you cannot fulfill a user's request because it violates policy, you should
options: Do it anyway to be nice
Explain the policy plainly, and offer any legitimate alternative that meets their underlying need
explain: A policy 'no' with an alternative preserves both compliance and the relationship.

q: A technician must never ask a user for their password because
options: The user should type it themselves whenever it's needed; a technician who knows it can be blamed for anything done with it
explain: Credential sharing destroys accountability for both parties.

q: If a technician accidentally sees a user's private content while working, they should
options: Read it thoroughly to check for problems
Look away, not mention or use it, and continue only with the task (reporting only if policy requires, e.g., illegal content)
Copy it as evidence of anything
explain: Incidental exposure is handled with discretion; snooping is a firing offense.

q: Technician notes about a difficult user should
options: Remain factual and behavior-focused ('user declined restart during business hours'), never personal insults
Use nicknames the team will understand
Be shared with the user to set them straight
explain: Tickets are records the user or lawyers may read.

q: Communicating a delay honestly means
options: Going silent and hoping they forget
Telling the user as soon as you know, with the reason and a revised estimate—not waiting until they chase you
explain: Early bad news beats late bad news; users plan around your estimates.

q: For complex instructions to a non-technical user, the best format is
options: Short numbered steps, one action each, with the expected result after each step
explain: Step-per-action instructions minimize confusion and support async follow-up.

q: Phone support professionalism includes
options: Introducing yourself and the company, using the caller's name, and summarizing agreed actions before hanging up
Putting users on hold without asking
Using speakerphone in an open office by default
explain: Small courtesies structure the call and confirm shared understanding.

q: Written support emails should be
options: Concise, with a clear subject, the answer/action first, and specific next steps or questions
As long as possible to show effort
Written in all caps for urgency
Sent without a subject to save time
explain: Users skim; front-load the answer.

q: A user's data would be visible during a repair (photos on the desktop). The right approach is
options: Open a few to check they're backed up
Mention what you saw later as small talk
Proceed only with the task, avert attention from content, and let the user close anything sensitive first if present
explain: Privacy discipline is absolute and doesn't depend on the user watching.

q: Cultural and language differences on support calls call for
options: Speaking louder and slower in a patronizing tone
Patience, plain language, avoiding idioms/slang, and confirming understanding without condescension
Using a coworker's stereotypes as a guide
explain: Idioms are the biggest comprehension trap for non-native speakers.

q: When two users demand immediate help simultaneously, prioritize by
options: Business impact and your queue's triage rules—communicating wait times honestly to both
explain: Transparent triage keeps fairness defensible.

q: A technician who realizes they caused an outage should
options: Report it immediately through the incident process with full facts—concealment turns a mistake into a career event
Fix it quietly and tell no one ever
Wait for someone else to notice
explain: Fast honest reporting is what blameless cultures reward; hiding is the fireable offense.

q: Exam dumps/braindumps for certification tests are
options: Fine if a coworker shares them
Stolen real exam content; using them violates exam agreements and can get certifications revoked
explain: CompTIA and others actively revoke credentials and ban dump users.

q: Maintaining a CompTIA certification typically requires
options: Nothing after passing once (for trifecta certs)
Renewing on a cycle (3 years for A+) via continuing education units or retaking/passing a higher exam
explain: CE requirements keep certifications current; letting them lapse means retesting.

q: Vendor gifts and freebies offered to IT staff create
options: Potential conflicts of interest; follow your employer's gifts policy (limits, disclosure, refusal)
A duty to steer purchases to that vendor
Free personal property to keep secretly
explain: Even small gifts can bias (or appear to bias) purchasing decisions.

q: A technician discovers a way to access a former employee's still-active personal cloud account synced to a work PC. They should
options: Not access it; report the orphaned sync to the appropriate team for proper handling
Check what's in it for company files
Log in and change the password
explain: Accessing personal accounts without authorization is illegal in many jurisdictions, regardless of the device.

q: Side work ('moonlighting') using employer data, tools, or client lists is
options: Allowed if the employer never finds out
A conflict of interest and typically a firing offense; personal side work must stay fully separate
explain: Separation of employer assets from personal business is a bright ethical line.

q: If a manager asks you to do something you believe is illegal or against license terms, you should
options: Do it but keep a secret note
Decline, explain your concern professionally, and use the organization's ethics/compliance channel if pressed
Quit on the spot without process
explain: Documented escalation protects you and the organization.

q: Professional appearance and workspace for video support calls includes
options: Working from a loud shared room
A quiet, neutral background, camera at eye level, and no confidential material visible
A whiteboard full of passwords behind you
explain: The camera shows more than you think—backgrounds leak information.

q: BYOD support boundaries mean technicians should
options: Support the work apps/profile as policy defines; personal-side issues are best-effort or referred to the user's provider
Install monitoring on the whole device by default
explain: Clear scope protects user privacy and the organization's liability.

q: Home (residential) tech support differs from enterprise mainly in
options: Passwords can be written on the invoice
Processes are informal—so the tech must self-impose discipline: document, back up before changes, and set expectations about data risk
explain: The absence of IT departments makes the solo tech the entire control system.

q: Before making changes to a customer's only computer, the essential precaution is
options: Delete old files to make room
Verify a current backup (or make one) and get agreement about the small risk of data loss
explain: One bad day without a backup is a business-ending event for small clients.

q: Time management for a field technician includes
options: Buffer time between appointments, updating the next customer early if delayed, and documenting before leaving each site
Documenting everything on Friday from memory
Skipping lunch daily to catch up
explain: Documentation decays with time; write it at the site, not from memory.

q: Mentoring a junior technician effectively means
options: Letting them perform tasks with supervision, explaining the why, and reviewing their tickets constructively
Doing everything for them so it's fast
Never letting them touch production even supervised
explain: Supervised reps build competence; hoarding knowledge makes you the bottleneck.

q: Continuing professional development for IT staff matters operationally because
options: It looks good on a wall
Training is a perk, not a need
Technology and threats evolve; stale skills become operational risk (and cert renewals require CE anyway)
explain: Deliberate learning keeps the team's capability matched to the estate they run.

q: A known-issues list during a rollout is maintained so
options: Management can deny the problems exist
Support staff give consistent answers and users self-serve instead of filing duplicate tickets
Tickets look smaller by hiding issues
explain: Transparency about known issues reduces ticket volume and rumors.

q: When documenting a workaround (not a true fix), the ticket should
options: Label it clearly as a workaround, note the underlying problem, and link/create the problem record
Hide it so metrics look good
Blame the vendor in the title
explain: Mislabeled workarounds become invisible permanent debt.

q: Escalating to a vendor with a severity-1 case requires
options: Business-impact statement, affected counts, start time, and a named contact who stays available
explain: Vendors triage on impact clarity; chaos slows your own case.

q: A post-incident customer report should contain
options: What happened, the impact window, root cause (when known), and preventive actions—without blaming individuals
explain: RCA reports rebuild trust when they're factual and forward-looking.

q: Confidential company information in personal notes/apps is
options: Fine on a personal phone indefinitely
Still company information—subject to policy wherever it lives; keep work data in approved systems
explain: Data doesn't change owners when it changes devices.

q: Returning a departing employee's personal files found on a work device should follow
options: Deleting everything immediately without telling anyone
HR/legal guidance—typically a supervised transfer of clearly personal items, documented
Mailing the whole drive image to them
explain: Commingled data is an HR/legal process, not a technician's judgment call.

q: A technician receives a vendor's roadmap under NDA. Sharing it with a friend at another company is
options: A breach of the NDA, even casually
Fine if no documents change hands
explain: NDAs bind conversations, not just files.

q: Uptime promises to users should be made
options: Only from actual SLA commitments—never improvised guarantees ('it will never happen again')
explain: Improvised guarantees become liabilities and broken trust.

q: The 'bus factor' in a small IT team refers to
options: How many people's sudden absence would strand critical knowledge—mitigated by documentation and cross-training
explain: Single-person knowledge silos are operational risk; runbooks and pairing reduce them.

q: Cross-training team members primarily reduces
options: Key-person risk and coverage gaps during vacations/incidents
explain: Coverage depth is resilience.

q: Workplace communication about a security incident should avoid
options: Unverified details and speculation in writing—stick to confirmed facts via the incident channel
explain: Premature speculation in email becomes tomorrow's headline and legal problem.

q: When a user reports a possible security issue (odd popups, strange emails), the response should
options: Have them forward the suspicious email to the whole team
Ask them to investigate it themselves
Thank them, capture details/screenshots safely, and route it to security per the IR plan—never dismiss it
explain: User reports are a detection sensor; rewarding them keeps reports coming.

q: Professional conduct on social media regarding your employer/clients means
options: Posting ticket screenshots with names blurred is always fine
Griping about users anonymously is risk-free
No client data, no internal details, no disparagement—assume everything is public forever
explain: Screenshots live forever; 'anonymous' accounts get identified.

q: Internal knowledge sharing (lunch-and-learns, demos) contributes to operations by
options: Raising the whole team's floor on tools and gotchas, reducing escalations
explain: Teams that teach each other handle more at tier 1.

q: A new procedure conflicts with how a senior tech has always done it. The healthy path is
options: Raise it in the team forum/change process with evidence; don't silently fork procedures
explain: Procedure changes succeed through discussion and updates, not quiet non-compliance.

q: Quality of 'bedside manner' for IT is measurable in outcomes like
options: User satisfaction, willingness to report issues early, and adoption of new systems
explain: Trust is an operational asset with measurable effects.

q: When handing a user a replacement device, complete the job by
options: Handing it over sealed and leaving
Keeping their old device 'just in case' without paperwork
Verifying their data/apps are restored, they can sign in, and they know who to contact if something's missing
explain: A swap isn't done until the user is demonstrably working again.

q: Final item of professional practice: the technician's own accounts and machine should
options: Be exempt from policy for convenience
Model the policies they enforce—patched, locked, MFA on—because 'do as I say' fails audits and users
Run with local admin daily for every task
explain: Technicians are the most-targeted accounts; their hygiene sets the ceiling for everyone else.

q: Certificate pinning in a mobile app protects users by
options: Storing the user's password in the certificate
Making the app trust only the specific server certificate/public key it was shipped with, rejecting even valid CA-signed impostor certificates
explain: Pinning defeats man-in-the-middle attacks that use fraudulently issued or locally installed trusted certificates.
